meaning: to ignore something you know is wrong
nomenclature_reason: It pictures someone closing their eyes so they can't see the problem, as if the eye is blind.
example: The librarian turned a blind eye when the kids whispered in the reading room.
remember: If you close your eyes, you pretend you didn't see.
correct_sentence: Maya turned a blind eye when she saw her friend copy an answer.
wrong_sentence: Maya turned a blind eye so she could see the board more clearly.

idiom: bite off more than you can chew
meaning: to take on a task that is too big or difficult
nomenclature_reason: It likens trying to chew a huge bite of food that won't fit in your mouth.
example: She tried to organize the whole school fair alone and soon realized she had bitten off more than she could chew.
remember: Don't try to chew a bite that's bigger than your mouth.
correct_sentence: Leo joined three clubs at once and soon saw he had bitten off more than he could chew.
wrong_sentence: Leo bit off more than he could chew, which only meant his sandwich was too big.

idiom: let the cat out of the bag
meaning: to reveal a secret by accident
nomenclature_reason: Imagine a cat hidden in a bag; when the bag opens, the cat jumps out and everyone sees it.
example: Tom let the cat out of the bag when he mentioned the surprise party to Sarah.
remember: When the cat jumps out, the secret is out.
correct_sentence: Aisha let the cat out of the bag by whispering the birthday plan in the hallway.
wrong_sentence: Aisha let the cat out of the bag so the kitten could play in the yard.

idiom: hit the nail on the head
meaning: to describe something exactly right
nomenclature_reason: It pictures a hammer striking a nail perfectly, so the job is done with one blow.
example: When Maya said the project needed more planning, she hit the nail on the head.
remember: A perfect hammer hit means a perfect answer.
correct_sentence: When Omar said the team needed a captain, he hit the nail on the head.
wrong_sentence: Omar hit the nail on the head, and the wooden birdhouse finally stayed together.

idiom: cost an arm and a leg
meaning: to be very expensive
nomenclature_reason: It imagines having to give up something as valuable as your arm and leg to pay for it.
example: The new video game console cost an arm and a leg, so I saved my allowance for months.
remember: If it needs an arm and a leg, it's super pricey.
correct_sentence: Those concert tickets cost an arm and a leg, so we watched from the park instead.
wrong_sentence: The bike cost an arm and a leg, which meant it was cheap enough for one week's allowance.

meaning: to make more effort than is expected
nomenclature_reason: It pictures walking farther than the distance you were asked to travel.
example: The teacher went the extra mile by giving us extra practice worksheets.
remember: Walk farther than asked to help others.
correct_sentence: Noah went the extra mile and walked the new student to every classroom.
wrong_sentence: Noah went the extra mile because the race was longer than one mile.

meaning: to hope that something will happen the way you want
nomenclature_reason: Crossing fingers is a old habit that people believed would bring good luck.
example: I kept my fingers crossed that I would win the spelling bee.
remember: Crossed fingers bring hopeful wishes.
correct_sentence: I kept my fingers crossed that the rain would stop before the picnic.
wrong_sentence: I kept my fingers crossed so my hands would stay warm outside.

idiom: have a chip on your shoulder
meaning: to be angry about something that happened in the past
nomenclature_reason: It comes from the old idea of carrying a small piece of wood (a chip) as a sign of being ready to fight.
example: After losing the game, Jake had a chip on his shoulder and didn't want to play.
remember: A chip on the shoulder means you feel upset about something.
correct_sentence: Priya had a chip on her shoulder after being left out of the game last week.
wrong_sentence: Priya had a chip on her shoulder because a crumb from her snack stuck to her shirt.

meaning: to avoid talking directly about something
nomenclature_reason: It comes from hunters who would walk around a bush instead of going straight to the animal.
example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what you really think.
remember: Going around the bush means not saying it straight.
correct_sentence: Stop beating around the bush and say which game you want to play.
wrong_sentence: They were beating around the bush while they searched for the lost ball.

meaning: to be in trouble
nomenclature_reason: Imagine being stuck in boiling water-it's uncomfortable and hard to get out of.
example: Sam was in hot water after he forgot to do his homework.
remember: Hot water means you're in a sticky spot.
correct_sentence: Ben was in hot water after he borrowed the tablet without asking.
wrong_sentence: Ben was in hot water because the bathtub was finally warm enough.

meaning: to make a bad situation worse
nomenclature_reason: If you pour more fuel on a fire, it burns brighter and hotter.
example: His teasing only added fuel to the fire during the argument.
remember: More fuel makes the fire grow bigger.
correct_sentence: Laughing at Mia's mistake only added fuel to the fire.
wrong_sentence: Dad added fuel to the fire so the campfire would cook the marshmallows.

meaning: to become nervous before doing something important
nomenclature_reason: It pictures your feet feeling cold because you are scared to move forward.
example: She got cold feet right before her big piano recital.
remember: Cold feet mean you feel shaky about trying.
correct_sentence: Jonas got cold feet and asked to skip his turn on the talent-show stage.
wrong_sentence: Jonas got cold feet because he forgot his socks on the snowy walk.

meaning: to avoid causing trouble by not bringing up old problems
nomenclature_reason: If a dog is sleeping, waking it might cause a bark or bite, so it's safer to leave it alone.
example: I decided to let sleeping dogs lie and didn't mention the argument from last week.
remember: Leave the sleeping dog alone so nothing wakes up.
correct_sentence: I let sleeping dogs lie and did not bring up the old argument at dinner.
wrong_sentence: I let sleeping dogs lie so the puppy could finish its nap on the couch.

meaning: to get to the important part without delay
nomenclature_reason: It comes from movies where you skip the long build-up and go straight to the exciting chase scene.
example: Can you cut to the chase and tell me what happened?
remember: Skip the intro and go straight to the action.
correct_sentence: Can you cut to the chase and tell us who won the race?
wrong_sentence: We cut to the chase by running the shortcut through the park.

idiom: be a fly on the wall
meaning: to wish you could watch a situation without being noticed
nomenclature_reason: A tiny fly can sit on a wall and see everything without anyone seeing it.
example: I wish I could be a fly on the wall during the secret meeting.
remember: A fly on the wall watches quietly without being seen.
correct_sentence: I wish I could be a fly on the wall when the judges pick the winner.
wrong_sentence: A fly on the wall kept buzzing, so we opened a window.

meaning: feeling sick or not feeling well
nomenclature_reason: When the weather is bad, it feels like a rainy cloud is covering you, so you are 'under' it
example: I think I'm under the weather, so I'll stay home from school.
remember: If you feel sick, you might be under the weather.
correct_sentence: Lila stayed home because she felt under the weather.
wrong_sentence: The kite flew under the weather, just below the clouds.

meaning: something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
nomenclature_reason: It sounds like a hidden gift, like a present wrapped in something that looks plain
example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise because I found a better one.
remember: Bad looks can hide good surprises.
correct_sentence: Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise, because I found my lost book at the stop.
wrong_sentence: The sunny picnic was a blessing in disguise, since everything went perfectly.

meaning: something that happens very rarely
nomenclature_reason: Blue moons are rare, so the phrase shows how uncommon the event is
example: We only get pizza for dinner once in a blue moon.
remember: Rare events are once in a blue moon.
correct_sentence: Grandpa visits our town only once in a blue moon.
wrong_sentence: We see a full moon once in a blue moon, every single month.

meaning: only a small, visible part of a much larger problem
nomenclature_reason: Only the top of an iceberg shows above water, hiding the big part below
example: The broken vase is just the tip of the iceberg; there are many more problems at home.
remember: What you see may be just a tiny tip.
correct_sentence: The messy desk was just the tip of the iceberg; the whole closet was overflowing.
wrong_sentence: The tip of the iceberg was the only part the ship needed to steer around, and the rest was tiny.

meaning: reverse a situation so the opposite side now has the advantage
nomenclature_reason: Imagine a table being flipped, changing who sits where
example: She turned the tables by answering his question first.
remember: Flipping the table flips the outcome.
correct_sentence: Nina turned the tables by asking her brother the riddle he had asked her.
wrong_sentence: Nina turned the tables so the guests could sit on the other side.

meaning: start something quickly and successfully
nomenclature_reason: Like landing and immediately sprinting, you begin fast
example: On his first day, Tom hit the ground running and finished the project.
remember: Start fast like running right after landing.
correct_sentence: On the first day of camp, Sofia hit the ground running and learned every trail name.
wrong_sentence: Sofia hit the ground running when she tripped at the start of the race.

idiom: keep one's eye on the prize
meaning: stay focused on the goal
nomenclature_reason: Like watching a prize you want, you never look away
example: She kept her eye on the prize and studied hard for the exam.
remember: Look at the prize and don't get distracted.
correct_sentence: He kept his eye on the prize and practiced the song every afternoon.
wrong_sentence: He kept his eye on the prize sticker so nobody would peel it off the box.

meaning: do something quickly and cheaply, often lowering quality
nomenclature_reason: Imagine cutting off the corners of a shape to make it smaller faster
example: The builder cut corners, and the house started leaking.
remember: Cutting corners can make things weaker.
correct_sentence: The poster team cut corners, and the paint peeled off the next day.
wrong_sentence: We cut corners on the paper to make neat triangles for the collage.

meaning: to fail or to stop working
nomenclature_reason: Picture someone falling to the ground and dust rising, showing something has ended
example: The old car finally bit the dust after years of use.
remember: When something bites the dust, it's finished.
correct_sentence: The old scooter finally bit the dust and would not roll anymore.
wrong_sentence: The puppy bit the dust on the path and sneezed.

meaning: give up or quit
nomenclature_reason: In boxing, a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight
example: After many tries, she threw in the towel and asked for help.
remember: Throwing a towel means stopping.
correct_sentence: After three failed tries at the puzzle, Eli threw in the towel.
wrong_sentence: After swimming, Eli threw in the towel so it would dry on the rack.

meaning: be very kind and generous
nomenclature_reason: Gold is precious, so a heart made of gold shows great value
example: My grandma has a heart of gold; she always helps others.
remember: A golden heart means big kindness.
correct_sentence: Mr. Patel has a heart of gold and stays late to help anyone who is stuck.
wrong_sentence: Mr. Patel has a heart of gold jewelry that he wears to the school play.

meaning: be in a risky or dangerous situation
nomenclature_reason: Walking on thin ice could break, showing danger
example: Skipping homework puts you on thin ice with the teacher.
remember: Thin ice means you could slip.
correct_sentence: Forgetting two quizzes in a row put Amir on thin ice.
wrong_sentence: Amir skated on thin ice at the rink and loved how smooth it felt.

meaning: keep talking about or trying something that's already decided
nomenclature_reason: A dead horse can't move, so beating it does nothing
example: We've already decided, so stop beating a dead horse.
remember: Beating a dead horse won't change anything.
correct_sentence: We already chose the team name, so stop beating a dead horse.
wrong_sentence: Beating a dead horse is how the riders wake it up for the parade.

meaning: be the person who decides what happens
nomenclature_reason: In old movies, the person who fires the gun decides the action
example: In our group project, Maya gets to call the shots.
remember: The one who calls the shots makes the plans.
correct_sentence: In the club, Rosa gets to call the shots about which game we play.
wrong_sentence: Rosa can call the shots because she is the best player at the basketball hoop.

idiom: take the bull by the horns
meaning: face a problem directly and bravely
nomenclature_reason: Grabbing a bull's horns shows courage because the bull is strong
example: He took the bull by the horns and talked to the principal.
remember: Grabbing the horns means being brave.
correct_sentence: He took the bull by the horns and told the coach he wanted a different position.
wrong_sentence: He took the bull by the horns at the farm and led it into the barn.

meaning: Working late into the night.
nomenclature_reason: In the past people used oil lamps; burning oil late means staying up working.
example: She had to burn the midnight oil to finish her science project.
remember: When you work late, think of a lamp burning all night.
correct_sentence: I had to burn the midnight oil to finish the diorama before morning.
wrong_sentence: We burn the midnight oil in the lamp so the porch stays lit all night.

idiom: The ball is in your court
meaning: It's your turn to decide or act.
nomenclature_reason: In tennis, after the ball lands in your side, you must hit it back.
example: I've given you the plan, now the ball is in your court.
remember: Like a tennis ball waiting for you to hit it.
correct_sentence: I sent you the choices, so now the ball is in your court.
wrong_sentence: The ball is in your court, so it is your turn to serve in tennis.

meaning: Find the hidden meaning that isn't said directly.
nomenclature_reason: Like looking at the blank spaces on a page to see a secret.
example: The teacher's note seemed simple, but you have to read between the lines.
remember: Look for the secret message in the quiet spaces.
correct_sentence: Her note sounded cheerful, but you have to read between the lines to see she is worried.
wrong_sentence: Read between the lines of the poem so you do not skip any printed words.

meaning: Small parts can cause big problems.
nomenclature_reason: A tiny mischievous devil hides in tiny details.
example: The recipe looks easy, but the devil's in the details.
remember: Tiny troublemakers hide in the little bits.
correct_sentence: The model looks simple, but the devil's in the details of those tiny wires.
wrong_sentence: The devil's in the details means a costume villain is hiding in the small print.

meaning: Take a risk without worrying.
nomenclature_reason: Imagine sending a careful warning note away on a gust of wind.
example: He threw caution to the wind and tried the new roller coaster.
remember: Let your worries fly away like a kite.
correct_sentence: She threw caution to the wind and tried the highest slide.
wrong_sentence: She threw caution to the wind by packing an umbrella for the storm.

meaning: Face a painful or difficult situation bravely.
nomenclature_reason: Soldiers used to bite a bullet during surgery to stay still.
example: She had to bite the bullet and tell the truth.
remember: Imagine biting a hard bullet to be brave.
correct_sentence: He had to bite the bullet and admit he broke the window.
wrong_sentence: He had to bite the bullet in the old story so the metal would not hurt his teeth.

meaning: Take a risk that could cause trouble.
nomenclature_reason: A sailboat near the wind may tip over.
example: He likes to sail close to the wind by breaking the rules.
remember: Like a boat almost tipping in a strong breeze.
correct_sentence: Skipping the safety check is sailing close to the wind.
wrong_sentence: The boat can sail close to the wind and still stay perfectly safe.

idiom: The writing is on the wall
meaning: A sign that something is going to happen, usually bad.
nomenclature_reason: Ancient stories had messages appearing on walls as warnings.
example: After the sales dropped, the writing was on the wall for the store.
remember: Imagine a warning scribbled on a wall.
correct_sentence: After three empty bake sales, the writing was on the wall for the club.
wrong_sentence: The writing was on the wall because the class painted a mural there.

idiom: Put the cart before the horse
meaning: Do things in the wrong order.
nomenclature_reason: A cart needs a horse to pull; putting it first makes no sense.
example: Planning the party before buying the cake is putting the cart before the horse.
remember: The horse should go first, not the cart.
correct_sentence: Buying decorations before we pick a theme is putting the cart before the horse.
wrong_sentence: Putting the cart before the horse helps the horse see where to pull.

idiom: Keep your nose to the grindstone
meaning: Work hard and stay focused.
nomenclature_reason: A grindstone is a tool; keeping your nose close means staying close to work.
example: If you keep your nose to the grindstone, you'll finish the puzzle fast.
remember: Stay as close to your work as a nose to a stone.
correct_sentence: Keep your nose to the grindstone and you will finish the model by Friday.
wrong_sentence: Keep your nose to the grindstone so the stone can sharpen it like a knife.

idiom: A stitch in time saves nine
meaning: Fixing a small problem early prevents bigger trouble later.
nomenclature_reason: One quick stitch now avoids needing many later.
example: Repairing the leak now is a stitch in time that saves nine.
remember: One tiny stitch now stops a big tear later.
correct_sentence: Patching the tent tonight is a stitch in time that saves nine.
wrong_sentence: A stitch in time saves nine needles, so bring extra thread to sewing class.

idiom: Don't count your chickens before they hatch
meaning: Don't assume something will happen before it actually does.
nomenclature_reason: You can't count chickens that aren't born yet.
example: He was already planning his vacation, but I told him not to count his chickens before they hatch.
remember: Wait until the eggs turn into chickens.
correct_sentence: Do not count your chickens before they hatch; you have not won the prize yet.
wrong_sentence: Count your chickens before they hatch so you know how many eggs are in the nest.

idiom: Let the chips fall where they may
meaning: Accept whatever result happens.
nomenclature_reason: When you chip wood, the pieces fall wherever; you can't control it.
example: She submitted her story and let the chips fall where they may.
remember: Like wood chips dropping wherever they want.
correct_sentence: She entered the contest and let the chips fall where they may.
wrong_sentence: She dropped the snack and let the chips fall where they may across the floor.

meaning: Sharing the same situation or problem.
nomenclature_reason: People in a small boat face the same water together.
example: All the students were late, so we were all in the same boat.
remember: Everyone rows together in one boat.
correct_sentence: The whole class missed the bus, so we were all in the same boat.
wrong_sentence: We were all in the same boat, rowing across the lake together.

meaning: Not decided yet; uncertain.
nomenclature_reason: Something floating in the sky hasn't landed yet.
example: Our weekend plans are still up in the air.
remember: Like a balloon drifting, not sure where it will go.
correct_sentence: Whether we go to the museum is still up in the air.
wrong_sentence: The kite is up in the air, so our plan is definitely happening.

idiom: The proof is in the pudding
meaning: You can only know if something works by trying it.
nomenclature_reason: The original saying was "the proof of the pudding is in the eating," meaning you have to taste the pudding to see if it's good.
example: We can only know if the new game is fun when we play it; the proof is in the pudding.
remember: Try it out to see if it works!
correct_sentence: We will not know if the shortcut works until we try it; the proof is in the pudding.
wrong_sentence: The proof is in the pudding, so the dessert tasted sweet and was finished.

idiom: A leopard can't change its spots
meaning: People cannot change their true nature.
nomenclature_reason: A leopard's spots are part of its skin and can't be removed, just like a person's basic traits.
example: Even after apologizing, he kept being selfish; a leopard can't change its spots.
remember: Some things stay the same, like a leopard's spots.
correct_sentence: He said he would share, then kept every marble; a leopard can't change its spots.
wrong_sentence: A leopard can't change its spots, so the zookeeper painted them a new color.

idiom: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
meaning: Don't risk everything on a single plan.
nomenclature_reason: If you drop one basket holding all the eggs, they all break; spreading them keeps some safe.
example: She saved money in both a bank and a piggy bank, because you shouldn't put all your eggs in one basket.
remember: Keep your eggs in many baskets.
correct_sentence: Do not put all your eggs in one basket; try out for two teams, not just one.
wrong_sentence: Put all your eggs in one basket so they are easier to carry from the shop.

idiom: Every cloud has a silver lining
meaning: Bad situations often have a hidden good side.
nomenclature_reason: When the sun shines behind a cloud, the edge looks bright like silver.
example: Even though the picnic was rained out, we got to play indoor games; every cloud has a silver lining.
remember: Look for the bright edge in a dark cloud.
correct_sentence: The game was canceled, but we baked cookies instead; every cloud has a silver lining.
wrong_sentence: Every cloud has a silver lining, so the sky stayed gray and nothing good happened.

idiom: The early bird catches the worm
meaning: People who start early get the best chances.
nomenclature_reason: Birds that wake up early find worms before others.
example: She arrived at the sale first and got the biggest discount; the early bird catches the worm.
remember: Get up early to get the prize.
correct_sentence: She lined up before the shop opened; the early bird catches the worm.
wrong_sentence: The early bird catches the worm, so birds that sleep late always get the best food.

idiom: You can't judge a book by its cover
meaning: Appearances don't show the true value.
nomenclature_reason: A book's cover may look plain, but the story inside could be wonderful.
example: He seemed shy, but he tells great jokes; you can't judge a book by its cover.
remember: Look inside before deciding.
correct_sentence: The scuffed violin sounded beautiful; you can't judge a book by its cover.
wrong_sentence: You can't judge a book by its cover, so always pick the book with the brightest jacket.

meaning: Waiting feels longer when you keep checking.
nomenclature_reason: If you stare at a pot, time seems to move slower, though the water boils at the same speed.
example: Stop checking the oven every minute; a watched pot never boils.
remember: Don't stare; let things happen.
correct_sentence: Quit staring at the download bar; a watched pot never boils.
wrong_sentence: A watched pot never boils, so staring at soup makes it cook faster.

meaning: What you do matters more than what you say.
nomenclature_reason: Loud sounds are heard better than quiet words; deeds are clearer than promises.
example: He promised to help, and then he actually cleaned the room; actions speak louder than words.
remember: Do it, don't just say it.
correct_sentence: He said he was sorry and then helped clean up; actions speak louder than words.
wrong_sentence: Actions speak louder than words, so a long speech matters more than helping.

idiom: All that glitters is not gold
meaning: Something that looks valuable may not be.
nomenclature_reason: Some shiny things look like gold but aren't really gold.
example: The toy looked fancy but broke quickly; all that glitters is not gold.
remember: Shiny isn't always real gold.
correct_sentence: The shiny compass broke on day one; all that glitters is not gold.
wrong_sentence: All that glitters is not gold, so anything sparkly is always valuable.

idiom: Cross that bridge when you come to it
meaning: Deal with problems when they happen, not before.
nomenclature_reason: You don't need to cross a bridge until you reach it.
example: We don't need to plan the trip's parking now; we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
remember: Handle it when you get there.
correct_sentence: We will cross that bridge when we come to it; no need to plan the ride home yet.
wrong_sentence: We will cross that bridge when we come to it, so let's map every bridge today.

idiom: Don't bite the hand that feeds you
meaning: Don't hurt those who help you.
nomenclature_reason: If you bite the hand giving you food, you lose the source of food.
example: She thanked her teacher instead of complaining; she didn't bite the hand that feeds her.
remember: Be kind to helpers.
correct_sentence: Do not bite the hand that feeds you by being rude to the neighbor who shares her garden.
wrong_sentence: Do not bite the hand that feeds you means keep your mouth closed while someone passes you bread.

idiom: Give the benefit of the doubt
meaning: Assume someone is innocent or right when you're not sure.
nomenclature_reason: You give them a "benefit" (a good point) when you don't have proof.
example: He might be late because of traffic, so we give him the benefit of the doubt.
remember: Think the best until you know.
correct_sentence: She might be late because of the bus, so let's give her the benefit of the doubt.
wrong_sentence: Give her the benefit of the doubt means we should assume she is definitely guilty.

meaning: Just before it is too late.
nomenclature_reason: "Nick" means a tiny cut; being saved by a tiny amount of time.
example: She submitted the homework in the nick of time before the deadline.
remember: Just in time!
correct_sentence: The doors were closing, and we slipped inside in the nick of time.
wrong_sentence: We arrived in the nick of time, hours after the show had ended.

idiom: Make a mountain out of a molehill
meaning: Exaggerate a small problem.
nomenclature_reason: A molehill is tiny, a mountain is huge; turning a tiny issue into a big one.
example: He got upset over a small mistake, making a mountain out of a molehill.
remember: Don't blow small things big.
correct_sentence: A spilled drop of paint is not a disaster; do not make a mountain out of a molehill.
wrong_sentence: Make a mountain out of a molehill when you want to shrink a huge problem.

meaning: Hard work is needed for success.
nomenclature_reason: You must feel some discomfort (pain) to achieve something valuable (gain).
example: She practiced piano daily; no pain, no gain.
remember: Work hard to win.
correct_sentence: Those extra laps were hard, but no pain, no gain.
wrong_sentence: No pain, no gain means the easiest practice gives you the biggest prize.

meaning: to take a risk by supporting something that might fail
nomenclature_reason: Imagine someone climbing a thin, far-out branch; if it breaks they could fall, so the picture shows taking a risk.
example: She went out on a limb and said she believed the new idea would work.
remember: Going out on a limb means being brave enough to try something risky.
correct_sentence: I went out on a limb and recommended the quiet new book to the whole class.
wrong_sentence: I went out on a limb of the oak tree to pick the highest apple.

meaning: to join others in doing something popular
nomenclature_reason: A bandwagon is a cart in a parade; when it moves, people hop on to be part of the fun, showing you follow the crowd.
example: When the new game became popular, many kids jumped on the bandwagon.
remember: Jump on the bandwagon when everyone else is doing it.
correct_sentence: Once the bead bracelets got popular, even the older kids jumped on the bandwagon.
wrong_sentence: They jumped on the bandwagon and rode it in the parade down the street.

meaning: to meet expectations or be good enough
nomenclature_reason: In old kitchens a sharp cut of mustard seed meant quality; if it 'cuts the mustard' it works just right.
example: The new teacher really cut the mustard and helped us learn.
remember: If something cuts the mustard, it does the job well.
correct_sentence: The backup goalie really cut the mustard and saved the match.
wrong_sentence: He cut the mustard and spread it on his sandwich at lunch.

idiom: burn the candle at both ends
meaning: to work or stay awake for too long, using up energy quickly
nomenclature_reason: A candle can only burn from one end; lighting both ends makes it finish faster, just like using too much energy.
example: He was burning the candle at both ends, studying all night and still going to soccer practice.
remember: Burning a candle at both ends means using up your energy fast.
correct_sentence: Soccer at dawn and homework at midnight means she is burning the candle at both ends.
wrong_sentence: Burning the candle at both ends makes the candle last much longer.

meaning: to blame or sacrifice someone to protect yourself
nomenclature_reason: Picture a bus driving by and someone being pushed under it; it shows an unfair blame.
example: When the project failed, the manager threw the intern under the bus.
remember: Throwing someone under the bus means blaming them to save yourself.
correct_sentence: When the poster ripped, Chris threw his partner under the bus and blamed her alone.
wrong_sentence: Chris threw his partner under the bus so she could catch a ride to school.

idiom: get a taste of your own medicine
meaning: to experience the same bad treatment you gave to others
nomenclature_reason: Medicine can be bitter; if you gave someone a bitter pill, feeling it yourself shows the meaning.
example: After teasing his friend, he got a taste of his own medicine when they teased him back.
remember: Taste your own medicine when you get treated the way you treated others.
correct_sentence: After hiding everyone's pencils, he got a taste of his own medicine when his vanished too.
wrong_sentence: He got a taste of his own medicine when the nurse gave him the syrup he liked.

meaning: to manage to survive or stay out of trouble, especially financially
nomenclature_reason: If you're swimming, keeping your head above water means you aren't sinking.
example: She works two jobs to keep her head above water.
remember: Keeping your head above water means not sinking.
correct_sentence: With two paper routes, she can just keep her head above water.
wrong_sentence: She can keep her head above water because she is a strong swimmer.

idiom: take the wind out of someone's sails
meaning: to make someone feel less confident or excited
nomenclature_reason: A sail needs wind to move; if the wind stops, the boat slows, just like a person losing enthusiasm.
example: His quiet answer took the wind out of her sails.
remember: When the wind leaves your sails, you feel less excited.
correct_sentence: The low score took the wind out of his sails after he had bragged all week.
wrong_sentence: The breeze took the wind out of his sails and pushed the boat even faster.

meaning: to start behaving in a better way
nomenclature_reason: A leaf turning green shows a fresh start, like opening a new chapter.
example: After the mistake, he decided to turn over a new leaf and study harder.
remember: Turning over a new leaf means starting fresh.
correct_sentence: After the messy project, he turned over a new leaf and labeled every folder.
wrong_sentence: He turned over a new leaf and found a beetle hiding under it.

meaning: to feel extremely happy
nomenclature_reason: Clouds are soft and high; being on the ninth cloud suggests floating high in joy.
example: She was on cloud nine after winning the spelling bee.
remember: Being on cloud nine feels like floating in big happiness.
correct_sentence: Winning the art ribbon put Maya on cloud nine.
wrong_sentence: The plane flew on cloud nine, which is just an ordinary cloudy day.

meaning: to watch carefully and be alert
nomenclature_reason: Peeling eyes like bananas is silly, but it means opening them wide to see everything.
example: Keep your eyes peeled for the missing puzzle piece.
remember: Peel your eyes open to see everything.
correct_sentence: Keep your eyes peeled for the green trail marker.
wrong_sentence: Keep your eyes peeled means rub them when they feel itchy.

idiom: have a foot in the door
meaning: to have a small start or opportunity that could lead to more
nomenclature_reason: Imagine a door slightly open with a foot inside; it shows a chance to go further.
example: Her internship gave her a foot in the door at the museum.
remember: Having a foot in the door means a small chance to get inside.
correct_sentence: Helping in the library gave her a foot in the door for the summer job.
wrong_sentence: She has a foot in the door because she forgot to close it behind her.

idiom: be a wolf in sheep's clothing
meaning: someone who looks harmless but is actually dangerous
nomenclature_reason: A wolf disguises itself as a gentle sheep to trick others.
example: The smooth salesman turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing.
remember: A wolf in sheep's clothing pretends to be nice but isn't.
correct_sentence: The smiling guide turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing and kept the map.
wrong_sentence: The farm dog wore a costume and looked like a wolf in sheep's clothing at the fair.

idiom: have a finger in every pie
meaning: to be involved in many different activities or projects
nomenclature_reason: Picture a pie with many fingers touching it, showing many connections.
example: She has a finger in every pie at the school, from clubs to sports.
remember: Having a finger in every pie means being part of many things.
correct_sentence: Jonah has a finger in every pie, from choir to the science fair.
wrong_sentence: Jonah has a finger in every pie, so his hands get sticky from the filling.

idiom: be a diamond in the rough
meaning: someone with great potential but still needs improvement
nomenclature_reason: A diamond hidden in rough stone needs polishing to shine.
example: The new student is a diamond in the rough; she just needs a little help.
remember: A diamond in the rough will shine after a little polishing.
correct_sentence: The shy drummer is a diamond in the rough and will shine with practice.
wrong_sentence: That rock is a diamond in the rough, already polished and ready to sell.

idiom: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree
meaning: Children often act or think like their parents.
nomenclature_reason: Just as an apple drops close to the tree it grew on, people usually resemble their family.
example: Sam is great at math, just like his dad; the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
remember: Kids grow like apples near their tree.
correct_sentence: Lila tells jokes just like her mom; the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
wrong_sentence: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree, so it rolled all the way down the hill.

idiom: the pot calling the kettle black
meaning: Criticising someone for a fault you also have.
nomenclature_reason: Both the pot and the kettle get black from fire, so it's silly for one to blame the other.
example: When Lily said Jake was messy, she was the pot calling the kettle black because her room is a mess too.
remember: Don't blame others for a flaw you share.
correct_sentence: Calling him noisy while you shout is the pot calling the kettle black.
wrong_sentence: The pot calling the kettle black means the kettle really is a darker color.

idiom: the squeaky wheel gets the grease
meaning: People who speak up about problems get attention and help.
nomenclature_reason: A wheel that squeaks is noticed and oiled, while quiet wheels are ignored.
example: Tom reminded the teacher about the broken projector; the squeaky wheel gets the grease.
remember: Speak up, like a squeaky wheel.
correct_sentence: She kept asking for a new net, and the coach replaced it; the squeaky wheel gets the grease.
wrong_sentence: The squeaky wheel gets the grease, so quiet people are always helped first.

idiom: the grass is always greener on the other side
meaning: We often think other people's situations are better than our own.
nomenclature_reason: From far away another lawn looks greener, even if it's not really.
example: Emma thought the new school would be better, but the grass is always greener on the other side.
remember: Every lawn looks greener from far away.
correct_sentence: He thought the other team had all the fun, but the grass is always greener on the other side.
wrong_sentence: The grass is always greener on the other side, so that lawn really does grow better.

idiom: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
meaning: It's safer to keep what you have than to risk losing it by chasing something better.
nomenclature_reason: Holding one bird is sure, while chasing two birds in the bushes might lose both.
example: Jake kept his part-time job instead of looking for a new one; a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
remember: Hold the bird you already have.
correct_sentence: Keep the sure part in the play; a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
wrong_sentence: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, so chase every maybe and drop what you have.

idiom: a rolling stone gathers no moss
meaning: Someone who keeps moving never settles down or builds lasting ties.
nomenclature_reason: A stone that rolls never stays still long enough for moss to grow on it.
example: Mia changes jobs every year; a rolling stone gathers no moss.
remember: Keep moving, and moss won't stick.
correct_sentence: They switch schools every year; a rolling stone gathers no moss.
wrong_sentence: A rolling stone gathers no moss, so it picks up more moss the farther it rolls.

idiom: a picture is worth a thousand words
meaning: A single image can convey a lot of information.
nomenclature_reason: Seeing a picture can tell a story faster than writing many words.
example: Instead of describing the map, the teacher showed a picture; a picture is worth a thousand words.
remember: One picture can tell many stories.
correct_sentence: One photo of the habitat said more than the paragraph; a picture is worth a thousand words.
wrong_sentence: A picture is worth a thousand words, so we should skip drawings and only write essays.

meaning: Being good at growing plants.
nomenclature_reason: A thumb that looks green from touching plants shows skill with gardening.
example: Grandma can make any flower grow; she really has a green thumb.
remember: Your thumb turns plants green.
correct_sentence: Every seedling she touches grows; she has a green thumb.
wrong_sentence: She has a green thumb because she spilled paint on her hand.

meaning: Someone who acts unpredictably and can cause trouble.
nomenclature_reason: A cannon that isn't fixed can roll around and fire at random places.
example: When Tom talks without thinking, he can be a loose cannon in class.
remember: A wandering cannon can fire anywhere.
correct_sentence: Blurting out the score early makes him a loose cannon.
wrong_sentence: A loose cannon on the old ship is a helpful tool that never causes trouble.

idiom: to be a bull in a china shop
meaning: Someone who is clumsy and breaks things in a delicate place.
nomenclature_reason: A big, strong bull would easily smash fragile china if it entered the shop.
example: Emily rushed through the art studio and knocked over the easels; she was a bull in a china shop.
remember: Big bull, tiny china-watch out!
correct_sentence: He charged through the pottery room like a bull in a china shop.
wrong_sentence: A bull in a china shop moves slowly and never bumps a single cup.

meaning: A person who stays up late and is active at night.
nomenclature_reason: Owls are birds that hunt and hoot when it's dark.
example: Sam reads books until midnight; he's a real night owl.
remember: Like an owl, you love the night.
correct_sentence: Kai reads until late and is a real night owl.
wrong_sentence: A night owl sleeps as soon as the sun goes down.

meaning: Very calm and relaxed, especially in a stressful situation.
nomenclature_reason: Cucumbers stay cool and fresh even when it's hot around them.
example: During the fire drill, Maya stayed as cool as a cucumber.
remember: Stay fresh like a cucumber.
correct_sentence: When the lights went out, Nia stayed as cool as a cucumber.
wrong_sentence: The cucumber in the fridge was as cool as a cucumber, which only describes the snack.

meaning: In very good health and physical condition.
nomenclature_reason: A well-made fiddle works smoothly and sounds perfect, just like a healthy body.
example: After his daily runs, Leo feels as fit as a fiddle.
remember: Your body can play like a perfect fiddle.
correct_sentence: After a summer of swimming, Theo feels as fit as a fiddle.
wrong_sentence: The fiddle is as fit as a fiddle because the case snaps shut.

meaning: Refusing to change your mind or give up, no matter what.
nomenclature_reason: Mules are known for not moving when asked, even if you pull hard.
example: Even after many hints, Maya kept her opinion; she's as stubborn as a mule.
remember: Mules won't budge, and neither do they.
correct_sentence: She would not switch seats no matter what; she is as stubborn as a mule.
wrong_sentence: As stubborn as a mule means she changes her mind every few minutes.

meaning: A clue or detail that misleads you from the real issue.
nomenclature_reason: In old stories, a smoked red herring was used to throw hunting dogs off the trail.
example: The detective realized the mysterious note was just a red herring.
remember: A smelly fish can lead you the wrong way.
correct_sentence: The muddy footprint was a red herring; the real clue was the open window.
wrong_sentence: A red herring is the useful clue that leads you straight to the answer.

meaning: Winning a battle but losing so much that it feels like a loss.
nomenclature_reason: Named after King Pyrrus who won a fight but his army was almost destroyed.
example: The team won the game, but many players got hurt, making it a Pyrrhic victory.
remember: Sometimes winning hurts more than losing.
correct_sentence: They won the relay, but three runners were hurt, so it was a Pyrrhic victory.
wrong_sentence: An easy win with everyone cheering is called a Pyrrhic victory.

meaning: To make an irreversible decision.
nomenclature_reason: Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon River, starting a war that couldn't be undone.
example: When she decided to move to another country, she crossed the Rubicon.
remember: Crossing the Rubicon means you can't go back.
correct_sentence: Sending the application yesterday means she crossed the Rubicon.
wrong_sentence: She crossed the Rubicon on the class hike and could still turn back anytime.

meaning: A small weakness in someone strong.
nomenclature_reason: In myth, Achilles was invincible except for his heel.
example: The superhero could lift cars, but his Achilles' heel was forgetting passwords.
remember: Even heroes have a tiny weak spot.
correct_sentence: The star speller's Achilles' heel is mixing up i and e.
wrong_sentence: An Achilles' heel is the strongest part of a hero.

meaning: Something that seems harmless but releases many problems.
nomenclature_reason: Pandora opened a box that let out all the world's troubles.
example: Downloading that unknown app was like opening Pandora's box.
remember: Opening Pandora's box lets trouble spill out.
correct_sentence: Opening that chain letter was like opening Pandora's box of rumors.
wrong_sentence: Pandora's box was a neat kit that solved every problem at once.

meaning: A constant feeling of danger.
nomenclature_reason: Damocles sat under a sword hanging by a single thread, showing how fragile safety can be.
example: The climber felt the Sword of Damocles while hanging on the ledge.
remember: A sword hanging above you means danger is close.
correct_sentence: Waiting to hear if the club would close felt like a Sword of Damocles.
wrong_sentence: A Sword of Damocles is a prize sword hanging safely on the wall.

meaning: Giving something valuable to someone who doesn't appreciate it.
nomenclature_reason: Pearls are precious; swine (pigs) can't understand their value.
example: He tried to explain the math, but it was like casting pearls before swine.
remember: Don't give treasures to those who can't see them.
correct_sentence: Explaining the poem to kids who only wanted jokes was casting pearls before swine.
wrong_sentence: Casting pearls before swine means sharing treasure with people who treasure it.

meaning: To add unnecessary decoration to something already perfect.
nomenclature_reason: A lily is beautiful; covering it with gold is overdoing it.
example: Adding glitter to the already bright drawing was gilding the lily.
remember: Don't over-decorate what's already beautiful.
correct_sentence: Stickers on an already perfect card are just gilding the lily.
wrong_sentence: Gilding the lily means the flower needed paint because it looked dull.

meaning: A job that never ends and feels pointless.
nomenclature_reason: Sisyphus rolled a stone up a hill only for it to roll back down forever.
example: Cleaning the messy room felt like a Sisyphean task.
remember: A Sisyphean task never really finishes.
correct_sentence: Raking leaves in a windstorm felt like a Sisyphean task.
wrong_sentence: A Sisyphean task is a short job you finish once and never repeat.

meaning: Being stuck between two dangerous choices.
nomenclature_reason: In Greek myth, sailors had to avoid the monster Scylla on one side and the whirlpool Charybdis on the other.
example: Choosing between lying and telling the truth put him between Scylla and Charybdis.
remember: Two dangers, pick the lesser one.
correct_sentence: Telling the truth or staying silent put him between Scylla and Charybdis.
wrong_sentence: Between Scylla and Charybdis means you have one easy, safe choice.

meaning: Fighting imaginary enemies or pointless battles.
nomenclature_reason: From Don Quixote, who imagined windmills were giants.
example: She kept trying to prove the rumor, tilting at windmills.
remember: Don't fight windmills that aren't real.
correct_sentence: Arguing with a rumor nobody believed was tilting at windmills.
wrong_sentence: Tilting at windmills means fighting a real enemy you can clearly see.

meaning: To challenge someone.
nomenclature_reason: Knights would throw a glove (gauntlet) to invite a duel.
example: He threw down the gauntlet and asked for a chess match.
remember: Throwing a gauntlet means saying 'I challenge you'.
correct_sentence: She threw down the gauntlet and challenged him to a spelling duel.
wrong_sentence: She threw down the gauntlet because the glove was dirty and she was done wearing it.

meaning: To start a complicated problem.
nomenclature_reason: Opening a can full of wriggly worms creates a messy situation.
example: Talking about money opened a can of worms at dinner.
remember: Opening the can makes a mess of problems.
correct_sentence: Asking who broke the lamp opened a can of worms at the table.
wrong_sentence: He opened a can of worms to feed the fish in the classroom tank.

meaning: Being drawn to something dangerous.
nomenclature_reason: Moths are attracted to bright flames even though they can get burned.
example: He kept checking the scary video, like a moth to a flame.
remember: Moths go to light even if it hurts.
correct_sentence: He kept replaying the scary clip like a moth to a flame.
wrong_sentence: A moth to a flame flies away from anything bright and risky.

meaning: To enter a strange, confusing, or endless situation.
nomenclature_reason: In Alice's story, she fell into a rabbit hole leading to a weird world.
example: Researching dinosaurs made her go down the rabbit hole of ancient history.
remember: A rabbit hole leads you deep into something weird.
correct_sentence: One video about caves sent her down the rabbit hole of underground rivers.
wrong_sentence: She went down the rabbit hole by hopping into a backyard burrow.

idiom: The pen is mightier than the sword
meaning: Writing can be more powerful than violence.
nomenclature_reason: A pen (words) can change minds more than a sword (force).
example: She solved the argument with a letter, proving the pen is mightier than the sword.
remember: Words can win more than weapons.
correct_sentence: A calm letter ended the fight, so the pen is mightier than the sword.
wrong_sentence: The pen is mightier than the sword means a sword always wins an argument.

meaning: something that looks harmless but hides a danger
nomenclature_reason: Greeks hid soldiers inside a wooden horse to enter Troy
example: The email looked friendly but was a Trojan horse containing a virus.
remember: A gift can hide secret soldiers.
correct_sentence: The cute link was a Trojan horse that hid a pop-up storm.
wrong_sentence: A Trojan horse is a friendly gift with nothing hidden inside.

meaning: a very difficult job that requires great strength
nomenclature_reason: Hercules performed twelve impossible labors
example: Building the new library was a Herculean task for the small town.
remember: Like Hercules, it needs super strength.
correct_sentence: Moving the whole library up the hill was a Herculean task.
wrong_sentence: A Herculean task is a quick chore a toddler could finish.

idiom: Rome wasn't built in a day
meaning: important things take time
nomenclature_reason: The great city of Rome took many years to become powerful
example: Learning to play the piano well takes practice; Rome wasn't built in a day.
remember: Big things need many days.
correct_sentence: Learning the violin takes months; Rome wasn't built in a day.
wrong_sentence: Rome wasn't built in a day, so famous cities appear overnight.

meaning: many different ways can reach the same goal
nomenclature_reason: In the old empire, many roads were built that all ended in Rome
example: Whether you study math or science, all roads lead to Rome if you want a career in engineering.
remember: Different paths can end at the same place.
correct_sentence: Flash cards or songs can both get you there; all roads lead to Rome.
wrong_sentence: All roads lead to Rome, so only one path can reach the goal.

idiom: When in Rome, do as the Romans do
meaning: follow the customs of the place you are in
nomenclature_reason: Visitors to Rome were expected to act like locals
example: He tried the local food because when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
remember: Copy what the locals are doing.
correct_sentence: At the host school we bowed with everyone, because when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
wrong_sentence: When in Rome, do as the Romans do means ignore local habits and keep your own.

meaning: something is completely confusing
nomenclature_reason: Ancient Greek was hard for many to understand
example: The math proof was all Greek to me.
remember: If it sounds like Greek, it's confusing.
correct_sentence: The code on the screen was all Greek to me.
wrong_sentence: It's all Greek to me means I understand every word of it.

meaning: a decision has been made that cannot be changed
nomenclature_reason: Caesar said "Alea iacta est" when he crossed the Rubicon, meaning the dice were thrown
example: After signing the contract, the die is cast.
remember: Once the dice roll, you can't pick them up.
correct_sentence: Once we mailed the form, the die is cast.
wrong_sentence: The die is cast means we can still change the decision tomorrow.

meaning: the ability to make money easily
nomenclature_reason: King Midas turned everything he touched into gold
example: The investor seemed to have the Midas touch, turning small ideas into big profits.
remember: Touch turns to gold like Midas.
correct_sentence: Every lemonade stand she opens earns money; she has the Midas touch.
wrong_sentence: The Midas touch means every project she starts loses money.

meaning: Something important has just begun.
nomenclature_reason: In old plays, a game starting was described as being 'afoot', meaning it is moving forward like a footstep.
example: When the treasure map was found, the game is afoot.
remember: When adventure starts, the game is afoot!
correct_sentence: The map is unfolded, so the game is afoot.
wrong_sentence: The game is afoot means the match ended hours ago.

meaning: Something that is certain to happen.
nomenclature_reason: Long ago people thought a conclusion that is already decided was already 'gone' before it was spoken.
example: The rain was a foregone conclusion after the dark clouds gathered.
remember: If you can see the ending already, it's a foregone conclusion.
correct_sentence: With that lead, her win was a foregone conclusion.
wrong_sentence: A foregone conclusion is a result nobody can predict.

idiom: born with a silver spoon in one's mouth
meaning: A person who is born into wealth or privilege.
nomenclature_reason: In old times, a silver spoon was a sign of riches, and being given one at birth showed great wealth.
example: She never had to work for money because she was born with a silver spoon in her mouth.
remember: A shiny spoon at birth means a rich start.
correct_sentence: He never saves allowance because he was born with a silver spoon in his mouth.
wrong_sentence: Born with a silver spoon in his mouth means he grew up with very little money.

meaning: To be the first to criticize or blame someone.
nomenclature_reason: In old stories, people would throw a stone at someone they thought was guilty; the first stone shows who starts the blame.
example: He shouldn't cast the first stone until he knows the whole story.
remember: The first stone thrown starts the blame game.
correct_sentence: Do not cast the first stone until you have heard her side.
wrong_sentence: Cast the first stone means throw the opening rock in a skipping contest.

meaning: A weak or false argument that is easy to defeat.
nomenclature_reason: People used to make a dummy out of straw to practice fighting; it was easy to knock down, just like a weak argument.
example: She built a straw man just to prove her point.
remember: A straw man falls down easily, just like a weak argument.
correct_sentence: He argued against an idea nobody had said; that was a straw man.
wrong_sentence: A straw man is the strongest, fairest version of the other person's point.

meaning: Someone who shows little emotion or warmth.
nomenclature_reason: A fish feels cold to the touch, so calling someone a cold fish means they seem unemotional.
example: Even after the surprise party, he acted like a cold fish.
remember: A fish feels cold, so a cold fish feels unemotional.
correct_sentence: Even at the party he stayed a cold fish and barely smiled.
wrong_sentence: A cold fish is someone who hugs everyone and laughs out loud.

meaning: A mean, dishonest, or contemptible person.
nomenclature_reason: In old sailor slang, 'scurvy' meant diseased, and a 'dog' was lowly, so together they described a nasty person.
example: Don't listen to that scurvy dog; he never tells the truth.
remember: A scurvy dog is a nasty, untrustworthy person.
correct_sentence: Do not trust that scurvy dog who keeps changing the score.
wrong_sentence: A scurvy dog is a loyal friend who always tells the truth.

meaning: A confusing or troublesome situation.
nomenclature_reason: In old markets, a kettle of fish could be messy; calling it 'fine' adds irony to the trouble.
example: When the lights went out during the play, it became a fine kettle of fish.
remember: A messy kettle of fish means a tricky situation.
correct_sentence: The missing costumes made opening night a fine kettle of fish.
wrong_sentence: A fine kettle of fish means everything is calm and easy to fix.

meaning: An achievement or honor that one can be proud of.
nomenclature_reason: Long ago hunters would put a bird feather in their hat as a trophy for a successful hunt.
example: Winning the spelling bee was a feather in her cap.
remember: A feather in your cap shows something you did well.
correct_sentence: Captaining the winning team was a feather in her cap.
wrong_sentence: A feather in her cap means a bird dropped a feather on her hat.

meaning: A futile or hopeless pursuit.
nomenclature_reason: People used to chase geese for sport, but the birds would fly away, making the chase useless.
example: Looking for the lost key under the couch was a wild-goose chase.
remember: Chasing a wild goose never catches anything.
correct_sentence: Searching the whole park for a key that was in her pocket was a wild-goose chase.
wrong_sentence: A wild-goose chase ends quickly because the goose waits in one spot.

meaning: Jealousy.
nomenclature_reason: Shakespeare called jealousy a monster that is green, like a jealous creature turning green with envy.
example: He felt the green-eyed monster when his friend got the new bike.
remember: Jealousy is the green-eyed monster inside us.
correct_sentence: The green-eyed monster showed up when his cousin got the bigger slice.
wrong_sentence: The green-eyed monster is a story creature with green eyes, not a feeling.

idiom: wear one's heart on one's sleeve
meaning: To show one's emotions openly.
nomenclature_reason: In old tournaments, a knight would tie a token of love to his sleeve, showing his feelings for all to see.
example: She wears her heart on her sleeve and cries easily during movies.
remember: If your heart is on your sleeve, everyone sees how you feel.
correct_sentence: He wears his heart on his sleeve and grins when he is proud.
wrong_sentence: Wear your heart on your sleeve means hide every feeling so nobody notices.

meaning: You have many opportunities and can achieve anything you want.
nomenclature_reason: Just as an oyster can hold a pearl, the world can hold wonderful things for those who look inside.
example: After graduation, the world is your oyster.
remember: A big world like an oyster can give you many pearls.
correct_sentence: With that scholarship, the world is your oyster.
wrong_sentence: The world is your oyster means you have almost no choices left.

meaning: A person who is very dear and cherished.
nomenclature_reason: Long ago, the pupil of the eye was called the 'apple' because it looked like a small round fruit; something precious to protect.
example: His little sister is the apple of his eye.
remember: The apple in your eye is something you love most.
correct_sentence: His little cousin is the apple of his eye.
wrong_sentence: The apple of his eye is the fruit he likes best at lunch.

meaning: Someone who prevents others from using something they don't need themselves.
nomenclature_reason: A dog might lie in a manger (where hay is stored) and stop cows from eating, even though the dog doesn't eat hay.
example: He keeps the video games locked away even though he never plays them-he's a dog in the manger.
remember: A dog in the manger blocks others, even if it doesn't need it.
correct_sentence: She will not lend the paints she never uses; she is a dog in the manger.
wrong_sentence: A dog in the manger shares the hay it does not need.

meaning: Being in a difficult or troublesome situation.
nomenclature_reason: The phrase comes from the idea of being stuck in a brine jar, which would be uncomfortable.
example: I forgot my homework, and now I'm in a pickle.
remember: If you're stuck like a cucumber in brine, you're in a pickle!
correct_sentence: I lost both shoes and now I am in a pickle.
wrong_sentence: In a pickle means you are relaxing with nothing to worry about.

meaning: A person who looks exactly like someone else.
nomenclature_reason: A "ringer" was a term for a duplicate, and "dead" means exact.
example: She is a dead ringer for her aunt.
remember: If you see a twin, it's a dead ringer!
correct_sentence: In that coat he is a dead ringer for his older brother.
wrong_sentence: A dead ringer is a broken doorbell that will not chime.

meaning: Someone who is used by another person to do a tricky or unpleasant job.
nomenclature_reason: In an old play a cat's paw was a paw used by a cat to fetch things for it.
example: The bully made him a cat's paw to deliver the note.
remember: If you're the cat's paw, you're doing the cat's dirty work.
correct_sentence: The older kids used him as a cat's paw to sneak the note into class.
wrong_sentence: A cat's paw is the soft paw of a kitten that does the work itself.

meaning: Something that is completely different from what was expected.
nomenclature_reason: Shakespeare used the phrase to describe a horse that was not the one being talked about.
example: Finding a bike is a horse of a different colour when we wanted a car.
remember: A different colour horse means a different kind of thing.
correct_sentence: Wanting a canoe when we planned a hike is a horse of a different colour.
wrong_sentence: A horse of a different colour is the same plan with a new name.

meaning: A big fuss over something very small.
nomenclature_reason: Imagining a huge storm inside a tiny teacup shows how exaggerated the worry is.
example: The argument over the missing crayon was just a storm in a teacup.
remember: A tiny teacup can't hold a real storm!
correct_sentence: Arguing for an hour over one marble was a storm in a teacup.
wrong_sentence: A storm in a teacup is a huge storm that floods the whole town.

meaning: A possession that is more trouble than it is worth.
nomenclature_reason: In royal courts a rare white elephant was costly to keep and hard to use.
example: The old computer became a white elephant because it broke all the time.
remember: A white elephant looks fancy but needs too much care.
correct_sentence: The giant aquarium was a white elephant we could not afford to keep.
wrong_sentence: A white elephant is a rare pet that is easy to care for and very useful.

meaning: Completely lifeless or not working.
nomenclature_reason: A doornail was hammered in so tightly it couldn't move, like being dead.
example: The battery is dead as a doornail.
remember: If it's as still as a nailed door, it's dead as a doornail.
correct_sentence: The flashlight is dead as a doornail and will not turn on.
wrong_sentence: Dead as a doornail means the battery is only a little low.

meaning: A task that is pointless or will not succeed.
nomenclature_reason: Sending a fool on a useless mission is a waste of effort.
example: Looking for a unicorn in the backyard is a fool's errand.
remember: A fool's errand is a wild goose chase without the goose!
correct_sentence: Hunting for a dragon in the schoolyard is a fool's errand.
wrong_sentence: A fool's errand is a task that is sure to succeed.

idiom: The lady doth protest too much
meaning: Someone who denies something so strongly it seems suspicious.
nomenclature_reason: From Shakespeare's play where a lady repeatedly says she doesn't love.
example: He kept saying he didn't take the cookie, but the lady doth protest too much.
remember: If you say "no" too many times, the lady doth protest too much.
correct_sentence: He denied it ten times; the lady doth protest too much.
wrong_sentence: The lady doth protest too much means a short, calm no is suspicious.

meaning: A final performance or act before retirement or death.
nomenclature_reason: Swans were once believed to sing a beautiful song just before they die.
example: The actor's last movie was his swan song.
remember: A swan's last song is its swan song.
correct_sentence: The coach's last game before retirement was her swan song.
wrong_sentence: A swan song is the first performance of a long career.

meaning: To raise a false alarm, causing others not to trust you later.
nomenclature_reason: From the story of a boy who shouted "wolf" when none came.
example: He kept saying the fire alarm was broken, and when it really rang, nobody believed him.
remember: If you keep shouting "wolf", people stop listening.
correct_sentence: If you cry wolf about fake fires, nobody will come when one is real.
wrong_sentence: Cry wolf means shout for help only when there is a real emergency.

meaning: Waiting anxiously or excitedly.
nomenclature_reason: "Bated" is short for "abated", meaning held back.
example: She waited with bated breath for the results.
remember: Hold your breath tight when you're excited!
correct_sentence: We waited with bated breath for the curtain to rise.
wrong_sentence: With bated breath means you are bored and barely paying attention.

meaning: Something that continuously provides profit or benefit.
nomenclature_reason: From the fairy tale where a goose laid golden eggs.
example: The garden became a golden goose, giving fresh veggies every day.
remember: A goose that lays gold makes a golden goose.
correct_sentence: The weekly comic booth became a golden goose for the club.
wrong_sentence: A golden goose is a bird that lays one egg and then stops forever.

meaning: A constant source of irritation or trouble.
nomenclature_reason: A thorn stuck in your side would keep hurting you.
example: The noisy neighbor was a thorn in his side.
remember: A thorn that pokes you is a thorn in the side.
correct_sentence: The dripping faucet was a thorn in his side all semester.
wrong_sentence: A thorn in his side is a small sticker he peeled off and forgot.

meaning: A hidden secret that could cause embarrassment if revealed.
nomenclature_reason: A skeleton hidden in a closet would be a shocking surprise.
example: The politician had a skeleton in the closet that the reporters discovered.
remember: A hidden skeleton is a skeleton in the closet.
correct_sentence: The old prank photo was a skeleton in the closet he hoped stayed hidden.
wrong_sentence: A skeleton in the closet is a Halloween decoration stored with the coats.

meaning: Respond to a hurtful act by not fighting back, but showing forgiveness.
nomenclature_reason: Jesus said if someone hits you, turn the other cheek so they have nowhere to hit you, showing kindness.
example: When Tom was teased, he turned the other cheek and smiled instead of arguing.
remember: If you turn the other cheek, you choose peace over a fight.
correct_sentence: When he was teased, he turned the other cheek and walked away.
wrong_sentence: Turn the other cheek means turn your face so you can shout back louder.

meaning: A person who helps strangers in need.
nomenclature_reason: From a Bible story where a Samaritan helped a hurt traveler while others ignored him.
example: Maya stopped to help the lost puppy; she was a Good Samaritan.
remember: A Good Samaritan is a kind helper you meet on the road.
correct_sentence: The stranger who returned the wallet was a Good Samaritan.
wrong_sentence: A Good Samaritan is someone who walks past a person who needs help.

meaning: People who don't know something trying to guide others who also don't know.
nomenclature_reason: Jesus warned that a blind person cannot lead another blind person without both stumbling.
example: The new student tried to teach the class, but it was a blind leading the blind situation.
remember: When the blind lead the blind, everyone trips.
correct_sentence: Two beginners teaching each other the map was the blind leading the blind.
wrong_sentence: The blind leading the blind means an expert is guiding a beginner.

meaning: A very dangerous or risky place.
nomenclature_reason: Daniel was thrown into a den of hungry lions but survived; the den is scary.
example: Going into the dark forest alone felt like entering a lion's den.
remember: A lion's den is a place where danger roars.
correct_sentence: Walking into the principal's office after the prank felt like a lion's den.
wrong_sentence: A lion's den is a cozy corner where nothing risky ever happens.

meaning: Someone who leaves home, wastes money, then returns humbled.
nomenclature_reason: A parable about a son who spent his inheritance and came back asking for forgiveness.
example: After spending all his allowance, Jake felt like the prodigal son when he asked his parents for help.
remember: The prodigal son learns that home is where love waits.
correct_sentence: After wasting his savings, he came home humble as the prodigal son.
wrong_sentence: A prodigal son is a child who never leaves home and never spends a cent.

meaning: A hero who rescues someone from trouble.
nomenclature_reason: Medieval knights wore bright armor and rode to save people in need.
example: When Lily fell, her friend acted like a knight in shining armor and helped her up.
remember: A knight in shining armor rides in to save the day.
correct_sentence: When her bike chain jammed, her friend was a knight in shining armor.
wrong_sentence: A knight in shining armor is someone who causes the trouble.

meaning: Plans or dreams that are unrealistic and unlikely to happen.
nomenclature_reason: Building a castle high in the sky is impossible, so the phrase means dreaming too big.
example: Sam wanted to own a dragon and a flying carpet-just castles in the air.
remember: Castles in the air are beautiful dreams that can't be built.
correct_sentence: A plan to live on the moon next week is castles in the air.
wrong_sentence: Castles in the air are solid plans you can start building today.

meaning: A male member of the clergy, like a priest.
nomenclature_reason: Clergy wear special cloth (robes) for their work, so they are called "men of the cloth."
example: Father Thomas is a man of the cloth who leads the Sunday service.
remember: A man of the cloth wears special robes and helps people pray.
correct_sentence: Father Ellis, a man of the cloth, led the holiday service.
wrong_sentence: A man of the cloth sews costumes and is not a clergy member.

meaning: Someone who comes to rescue or defend another, often in a bold way.
nomenclature_reason: Knights wore white armor to show purity and bravery, so a "white knight" is a brave rescuer.
example: When the bully tried to take her book, a classmate acted as a white knight and stopped him.
remember: A white knight rides in shining white to protect friends.
correct_sentence: When the books spilled, a classmate played white knight and helped her up.
wrong_sentence: A white knight is the person who starts the mess and walks away.

meaning: Something people search for because it is extremely valuable or perfect.
nomenclature_reason: In the legends, the Holy Grail was a sacred cup that knights sought; it represents the ultimate prize.
example: Finding a quiet place to read is the holy grail for busy kids.
remember: The holy grail is the most treasured thing you can imagine.
correct_sentence: A quiet reading nook is the holy grail for a busy family.
wrong_sentence: A holy grail is an ordinary cup nobody particularly wants.

meaning: The person who owns and runs a large estate or house.
nomenclature_reason: In medieval times, the lord owned the manor and made decisions for everyone living there.
example: In the story, the old oak tree was the lord of the manor of the forest.
remember: The lord of the manor is the boss of the big house.
correct_sentence: In the story the oak is the lord of the manor of the whole grove.
wrong_sentence: The lord of the manor is a guest who does not own the house.

meaning: To do something that creates many problems or conflicts.
nomenclature_reason: In a myth, planting dragon's teeth grew into armed warriors, so "sowing the dragon's teeth" means starting trouble.
example: Posting a mean comment online can sow the dragon's teeth and cause a big argument.
remember: When you sow dragon's teeth, you plant trouble that grows fast.
correct_sentence: That rude post can sow the dragon's teeth and start a huge fight.
wrong_sentence: Sow the dragon's teeth means plant a garden that grows only peace.

meaning: A friendly gesture that hides betrayal.
nomenclature_reason: Judas kissed Jesus to show loyalty while planning to betray him.
example: The new friend gave a Judas kiss when he promised to keep the secret but told the teacher.
remember: A Judas kiss looks kind but hides a backstab.
correct_sentence: The handshake was a Judas kiss; he had already told the secret.
wrong_sentence: A Judas kiss is a kind gesture that proves someone is loyal.

meaning: A huge amount of money.
nomenclature_reason: In old times, a king could demand a huge sum to free a captive; that sum became known as a king's ransom.
example: The rare comic book sold for a king's ransom at the auction.
remember: A king's ransom is a treasure worth a king's gold.
correct_sentence: The signed card sold for a king's ransom.
wrong_sentence: A king's ransom is a few coins, barely enough for a snack.

meaning: A person who is different from or disliked by the rest of a family or group.
nomenclature_reason: In a flock, a sheep with dark wool stands out; calling someone a black sheep means they stand out in a not-so-good way.
example: Tim felt like the black sheep because he liked painting instead of sports.
remember: A black sheep is the family member who looks different from the rest.
correct_sentence: She felt like the black sheep because she loved chess, not soccer.
wrong_sentence: The black sheep is the family member everyone copies and praises.

meaning: surprised or shocked by something unexpected.
nomenclature_reason: Ships used to be 'abaft' the wind; being taken aback meant the wind hit the front, stopping the ship suddenly, just like a surprise stops you.
example: She was taken aback when the magician made the rabbit disappear.
remember: Imagine a ship that stops suddenly because the wind hits it - that feeling is being taken aback.
correct_sentence: I was taken aback when the quiet kid won the loudest cheer.
wrong_sentence: Taken aback means you expected exactly what happened.

meaning: feeling bored, sad, or lacking energy.
nomenclature_reason: The doldrils are calm parts of the sea where there is no wind, so ships drift without moving, just like a person who feels stuck.
example: He felt in the doldrums after finishing his big project.
remember: Think of a boat stuck in a wind-less sea - that's being in the doldrums.
correct_sentence: After the festival he sat in the doldrums with nothing fun left to do.
wrong_sentence: In the doldrums means you are bursting with energy and excitement.

meaning: prepare for a difficult or dangerous situation.
nomenclature_reason: Sailors would secure the ship's hatches with battens to keep out stormy water, just like we get ready for trouble.
example: We need to batten down the hatches before the big exam tomorrow.
remember: When a storm comes, sailors close the hatches - that's getting ready for a challenge.
correct_sentence: We should batten down the hatches before the big recital.
wrong_sentence: Batten down the hatches means relax because no trouble is coming.

meaning: manage something with strict rules and good order.
nomenclature_reason: A well-run ship had tight ropes and clear commands, so everything worked smoothly.
example: The teacher runs a tight ship in her classroom.
remember: A ship with tight ropes stays steady - that's what running a tight ship means.
correct_sentence: Coach Diaz runs a tight ship and every cone is back in the bin.
wrong_sentence: Run a tight ship means let everyone do whatever they want.

meaning: to start moving or begin a new activity.
nomenclature_reason: Ships lifted (weighed) their heavy anchors to set sail, just like we lift a weight to start moving.
example: After the holidays, the students will weigh anchor and start the new term.
remember: When a ship lifts its anchor, it can go - that's weighing anchor.
correct_sentence: Monday we weigh anchor and start the new science unit.
wrong_sentence: Weigh anchor means stop a journey before it begins.

meaning: someone who does what they want without following rules.
nomenclature_reason: In old courts, a person who acted like their own judge was said to be a 'law unto themselves'.
example: He rides his bike wherever he likes; he's a law unto himself.
remember: Imagine a person writing their own rules - that's a law unto oneself.
correct_sentence: He parks his bike anywhere; he is a law unto himself.
wrong_sentence: A law unto himself follows every rule without being asked.

meaning: a very skilled and knowledgeable lawyer.
nomenclature_reason: Eagles soar high and see far, just like a sharp lawyer sees all the details of a case.
example: She became a legal eagle after years of studying law.
remember: Think of an eagle flying high and spotting everything - that's a legal eagle.
correct_sentence: After years of mock trials she became a legal eagle.
wrong_sentence: A legal eagle is someone who knows almost nothing about the law.

meaning: an issue that no longer matters or cannot be decided.
nomenclature_reason: In old debates, a 'moot' was a mock case for practice; if it was just for show, it was a moot point.
example: Whether we wear hats is a moot point now that school is over.
remember: A moot point is like a practice case - it doesn't affect the real outcome.
correct_sentence: Who sits where is a moot point now that the trip is canceled.
wrong_sentence: A moot point is the most important question we still must decide.

meaning: an example that clearly shows what is being discussed.
nomenclature_reason: Lawyers point to a specific case to illustrate a rule, so the example becomes the 'case in point'.
example: She loves reading; a case in point is her favorite book club.
remember: When a lawyer shows a case to prove a rule, that case is the case in point.
correct_sentence: She loves bugs; a case in point is the ant farm on her desk.
wrong_sentence: A case in point is an example that has nothing to do with the topic.

idiom: jack of all trades, master of none
meaning: someone who knows a little about many things but isn't an expert in any.
nomenclature_reason: In old guilds, a 'jack' was a worker who tried many crafts but never mastered one.
example: Tom can fix toys, bake cakes, and paint walls, but he's a jack of all trades, master of none.
remember: Picture a worker trying many jobs but not becoming a master of any - that's the meaning.
correct_sentence: He can bake, draw, and fix bikes, but he is a jack of all trades, master of none.
wrong_sentence: A jack of all trades, master of none is an expert at one single skill.

meaning: a person who is blamed for the problems of others.
nomenclature_reason: In ancient rituals, a goat was sent into the desert carrying the community's sins, becoming the scapegoat.
example: When the project failed, the intern became the scapegoat.
remember: Think of a goat carrying away all the blame - that's a scapegoat.
correct_sentence: When the display fell, the newest member became the scapegoat.
wrong_sentence: A scapegoat is the person who truly caused the problem and admits it.

meaning: someone who takes the blame for something they didn't do.
nomenclature_reason: In old street slang, the 'guy' who fell was the one caught and blamed.
example: The manager made the assistant the fall guy for the missing files.
