remember: Imagine someone tripping and getting blamed - that person is the fall guy.
correct_sentence: They made the quiet kid the fall guy for the missing markers.
wrong_sentence: A fall guy is the hero who takes credit for a success.

meaning: a thief who steals money from people's pockets.
nomenclature_reason: In old markets, pickpockets used a small 'cut' (knife) to open purses quickly.
example: The bustling fair attracted many cutpurses looking for easy loot.
remember: Think of a sneaky person cutting open a purse - that's a cutpurse.
correct_sentence: The crowded fair was full of cutpurses watching open backpacks.
wrong_sentence: A cutpurse is a person who sews purses and returns lost wallets.

meaning: to cause a change in a situation, especially for the better.
nomenclature_reason: Sailors watched the tide rise or fall; when it turned, the ship's direction changed.
example: Her kind words turned the tide of his bad mood.
remember: When the ocean tide flips, the water moves differently - that's turning the tide.
correct_sentence: One kind joke turned the tide and the argument cooled off.
wrong_sentence: Turn the tide means keep a bad situation exactly the same.

meaning: to pretend to be something you are not, especially to deceive.
nomenclature_reason: Pirates would raise a friendly flag (false colors) to get close before attacking.
example: The salesman tried to sail under false colors by claiming the toy was brand new.
remember: Picture a ship waving a friendly flag while hiding its true intent - that's sailing under false colors.
correct_sentence: He tried to sail under false colors by pretending the used bike was new.
wrong_sentence: Sail under false colors means show everyone exactly who you are.

meaning: a hidden, treacherous person
nomenclature_reason: Snakes hide in grass and can bite you when you least expect it, just like a secret betrayer.
example: She thought her friend was nice, but he turned out to be a snake in the grass.
remember: Remember the sneaky snake hiding in the grass when someone pretends to be friendly.
correct_sentence: The smiling teammate was a snake in the grass who copied her notes.
wrong_sentence: A snake in the grass is a friend who warns you about hidden trouble.

meaning: the biggest part of something
nomenclature_reason: A lion is the strongest animal in the jungle, so it would take the biggest piece of a meal.
example: When the cookies were divided, Tom got the lion's share because he helped bake them.
remember: Think of a lion taking the biggest bite of a big steak.
correct_sentence: Because she built the set, she got the lion's share of the applause.
wrong_sentence: The lion's share is the smallest piece left after everyone else picks.

meaning: an innocent person walking into danger without knowing it
nomenclature_reason: A lamb is gentle, and slaughter is a sudden end, so the picture means someone harmless is led into trouble.
example: The new student was a lamb to the slaughter when he walked into the surprise prank.
remember: A quiet lamb should not be led into a scary place.
correct_sentence: Walking into the surprise roast, he was a lamb to the slaughter.
wrong_sentence: A lamb to the slaughter knows the danger and comes prepared.

meaning: something bought or accepted without checking it first, which may turn out to be bad
nomenclature_reason: Long ago, merchants would sell a closed bag (a 'poke') that might contain a pig or something worthless.
example: He bought the game without reading reviews and got a pig in a poke.
remember: Imagine opening a bag expecting a toy but finding a pig instead.
correct_sentence: Buying the sealed box of games was a pig in a poke.
wrong_sentence: A pig in a poke is a gift you inspected carefully before accepting.

meaning: a foolish or poorly thought-out plan
nomenclature_reason: Hares are quick and jumpy, and a plan that jumps around without thinking is called harebrained.
example: Building a treehouse without nails was a harebrained scheme.
remember: Think of a hare bouncing around with a wild idea.
correct_sentence: Building a raft from cardboard was a harebrained scheme.
wrong_sentence: A harebrained scheme is a careful plan that is sure to work.

meaning: to decide not to do something because of fear
nomenclature_reason: Chickens are known to run away when they sense danger, just like a person who backs out of a challenge.
example: He wanted to jump off the high dive, but he chickened out at the last second.
remember: Remember a chicken running away when it's scared.
correct_sentence: He reached the high dive and then chickened out.
wrong_sentence: Chicken out means you feel brave and jump right away.

meaning: a very rare and unexpected event that has a big impact
nomenclature_reason: For centuries people thought all swans were white; a black swan was thought impossible until one was seen.
example: The sudden storm was a black swan that ruined the picnic.
remember: Picture a surprising black swan swimming where only white swans were expected.
correct_sentence: The surprise snow day was a black swan nobody had planned for.
wrong_sentence: A black swan is an ordinary event everyone saw coming.

meaning: Solve a complex problem with a bold, simple solution.
nomenclature_reason: Alexander the Great sliced the legendary knot instead of untying it, showing a clever shortcut.
example: When the computer crashed, Jamie cut the Gordian knot by reinstalling the whole system.
remember: When a puzzle looks impossible, think of a sharp cut like Alexander.
correct_sentence: She cut the Gordian knot by starting the story over instead of patching every plot hole.
wrong_sentence: Cut the Gordian knot means spend weeks on every tiny tangle.

meaning: Something very valuable or cherished.
nomenclature_reason: Ancient traders prized pearls like treasure from the sea, calling them priceless.
example: Grandma's old recipe book is a pearl of great price to the family.
remember: Think of a shining pearl you would never trade away.
correct_sentence: That handwritten songbook is a pearl of great price in our family.
wrong_sentence: A pearl of great price is a cheap bead nobody wants to keep.

meaning: Being ignored even when you warn others about danger.
nomenclature_reason: Cassandra, a prophetess in Greek myth, told the truth but nobody believed her.
example: When Lily warned about the storm, she felt she had a Cassandra complex when no one listened.
remember: Cassandra's warnings fell on deaf ears.
correct_sentence: She warned them about the loose step and felt she had a Cassandra complex when they laughed.
wrong_sentence: A Cassandra complex means everyone listens the moment you warn them.

meaning: Live with strict self-control and simplicity.
nomenclature_reason: Spartans were famous for their tough training and plain lives, never indulging in luxuries.
example: During the science fair prep, the team had to maintain Spartan discipline to finish on time.
remember: Think of a soldier who never relaxes - that's Spartan discipline.
correct_sentence: To finish the fair booth they had to maintain Spartan discipline and skip extra snacks.
wrong_sentence: Maintain Spartan discipline means relax the rules whenever you feel like it.

meaning: Lost at sea; dead or gone forever.
nomenclature_reason: Sailors believed the sea god Davy Jones kept drowned souls in his underwater chest.
example: The old pirate ship vanished and was said to be in Davy Jones' locker.
remember: If something sinks deep, it's in Davy Jones' hidden chest.
correct_sentence: The toy boat drifted off and was lost in Davy Jones' locker.
wrong_sentence: In Davy Jones' locker means the ship is safe in the harbor.

meaning: Encounter a problem that seems impossible to solve.
nomenclature_reason: The legendary knot was so tangled that only a bold cut could free it.
example: When the math puzzle got too tricky, Sam felt he had to face a Gordian knot.
remember: A knot so tangled you might need a clever cut.
correct_sentence: The tangled schedule made him face a Gordian knot.
wrong_sentence: Face a Gordian knot means the problem is simple and already solved.

idiom: hold the line like a Roman legion
meaning: Stay firm and unyielding in a difficult situation.
nomenclature_reason: Roman legions were famous for standing their ground without wavering.
example: During the debate, Maya held the line like a Roman legion and didn't back down.
remember: Think of brave soldiers who never move.
correct_sentence: In the debate she held the line like a Roman legion and would not give up her point.
wrong_sentence: Hold the line like a Roman legion means retreat as soon as questions start.

idiom: drink from the cup of Hyacinth
meaning: Enjoy a fleeting, beautiful moment that soon fades.
nomenclature_reason: Hyacinth was a beautiful youth whose life ended quickly, and his memory lived on in a flower.
example: The sunset was so gorgeous that it felt like drinking from the cup of Hyacinth.
remember: A beautiful sip that disappears fast.
correct_sentence: The firefly minute felt like drinking from the cup of Hyacinth.
wrong_sentence: Drink from the cup of Hyacinth means enjoy a moment that lasts forever.

idiom: march to the beat of a Roman drum
meaning: Follow a strict, orderly routine.
nomenclature_reason: Roman soldiers marched in perfect rhythm to the drum, never missing a step.
example: Every morning, Lily marched to the beat of a Roman drum, brushing her teeth and packing her bag.
remember: Imagine soldiers moving together on a drum's rhythm.
correct_sentence: Every morning he marches to the beat of a Roman drum: wash, pack, then out the door.
wrong_sentence: March to the beat of a Roman drum means ignore routines and wander all day.

meaning: I have many chances and can achieve anything I want.
nomenclature_reason: In Shakespeare an oyster can hold a pearl; the world is like a big oyster that can give you treasure.
example: When Lily got the scholarship, she said the world is my oyster.
remember: Think of a shiny pearl inside a huge oyster waiting just for you.
correct_sentence: After the award she said the world is my oyster.
wrong_sentence: The world is my oyster means almost every door is closed.

meaning: A silly or unbelievable tale.
nomenclature_reason: The phrase mixes a rooster (cock) and a bull, two unlikely animals trying to tell a story together.
example: Tom's excuse for being late was just a cock and bull story.
remember: Imagine a rooster and a bull trying to tell a tale - it must be a tall one!
correct_sentence: His story about a dragon eating his homework was a cock and bull story.
wrong_sentence: A cock and bull story is a report everyone knows is true.

meaning: A big fuss over something very small.
nomenclature_reason: A tempest is a huge storm, but here it is imagined inside a tiny teapot, showing the exaggeration.
example: She made a tempest in a teapot about the missing cookie.
remember: Picture a massive storm brewing inside a tiny teacup.
correct_sentence: She made a tempest in a teapot over one crooked nametag.
wrong_sentence: A tempest in a teapot is a huge disaster that hurts the whole town.

meaning: Someone who causes trouble or chaos in a calm place.
nomenclature_reason: Cats scare pigeons; putting a cat among them makes a noisy mess.
example: When Jake shouted, he was a cat among the pigeons in the quiet library.
remember: Think of a sneaky cat making the pigeons flutter.
correct_sentence: Yelling the score in the quiet room made him a cat among the pigeons.
wrong_sentence: A cat among the pigeons keeps a calm room even calmer.

meaning: To argue the opposite side just to test ideas.
nomenclature_reason: The devil is known for challenging good people; playing his role means questioning everything.
example: Even though she liked the plan, Maya decided to play devil's advocate.
remember: Pretend you're the devil asking, "what if…?"
correct_sentence: She liked the idea but played devil's advocate to test it.
wrong_sentence: Play devil's advocate means agree with every point and never question it.

meaning: To try to do something that is pointless.
nomenclature_reason: A fool goes on a task that leads nowhere, like chasing shadows.
example: Looking for a unicorn in the backyard was a fool's errand.
remember: Picture a silly person chasing something that isn't there.
correct_sentence: Searching the attic for a unicorn was going on a fool's errand.
wrong_sentence: Go on a fool's errand means take on a job that is sure to pay off.

meaning: A person who thinks they are the most important.
nomenclature_reason: A cock (rooster) struts proudly as if the whole street belongs to him.
example: After winning the race, he strutted like the cock of the walk.
remember: Imagine a proud rooster marching down the street.
correct_sentence: After one goal he strutted like the cock of the walk.
wrong_sentence: The cock of the walk is the quiet player who never boasts.

meaning: A sneaky person who causes trouble where they shouldn't.
nomenclature_reason: A fox in a henhouse will eat the chickens, causing chaos.
example: The new kid was a fox in the henhouse, stealing snacks.
remember: Imagine a clever fox sneaking into a chicken coop.
correct_sentence: Leaving him alone with the snack bin was a fox in the henhouse.
wrong_sentence: A fox in the henhouse is a careful guest who protects what is there.

idiom: to throw the baby out with the bathwater
meaning: to get rid of something good while trying to get rid of something bad
nomenclature_reason: If you tip out a washtub too fast, the baby could go out with the dirty water.
example: She deleted the whole folder to remove one bad photo and threw the baby out with the bathwater.
remember: Keep the baby when you pour out the dirty water.
correct_sentence: Deleting the whole album to remove one blurry photo threw the baby out with the bathwater.
wrong_sentence: Throw the baby out with the bathwater means toss only the dirty water and keep what is good.

meaning: Someone who feels uncomfortable in a new situation.
nomenclature_reason: A fish cannot breathe outside water, so it looks uneasy and out of place.
example: On her first day at the new school, Maya felt like a fish out of water.
remember: Imagine a fish flopping on dry land.
correct_sentence: At the new dance club she felt like a fish out of water.
wrong_sentence: A fish out of water is someone who feels right at home in a new place.

meaning: A great mismatch; two things that are completely unsuitable for each other.
nomenclature_reason: Roland was a mighty French hero, Oliver a small English one; putting them together shows they don't fit.
example: Giving a tiny toy car to a giant is a Roland for an Oliver.
remember: Big hero and tiny hero don't match, just like a Roland for an Oliver.
correct_sentence: Giving a tiny teacup to a giant is a Roland for an Oliver.
wrong_sentence: A Roland for an Oliver means two things that fit each other perfectly.

meaning: A luxury given to someone of high rank.
nomenclature_reason: Generals were served the finest foods, like caviare, to show respect.
example: The new computer was caviare to the general for the school principal.
remember: Fancy food for a fancy boss.
correct_sentence: The fancy microscope was caviare to the general, saved for the head of the lab.
wrong_sentence: Caviare to the general means a plain snack shared with everyone equally.

meaning: A person who is very wise and just, especially in a courtroom.
nomenclature_reason: Daniel in the Bible was known for his wise decisions before kings.
example: The teacher was a Daniel come to judgement when she settled the playground dispute.
remember: Think of Daniel the wise judge.
correct_sentence: When she settled the argument fairly, she was a Daniel come to judgement.
wrong_sentence: A Daniel come to judgement is someone who picks a side without listening.

idiom: more honoured in the breach than the observance
meaning: A rule is better broken than followed.
nomenclature_reason: If breaking a rule makes you look better, the breach is more honoured.
example: Skipping bedtime on a school night is more honoured in the breach than the observance.
remember: Sometimes breaking a rule looks better.
correct_sentence: That outdated hallway rule is more honoured in the breach than the observance.
wrong_sentence: More honoured in the breach than the observance means everyone should follow the rule strictly.

idiom: run with the hare and hunt with the hounds
meaning: To try to please both sides of a conflict, often ending up in trouble.
nomenclature_reason: Hares run away while hounds chase; doing both puts you in danger from each.
example: She tried to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds, pleasing both groups but making no one trust her.
remember: Being on both sides can get you caught.
correct_sentence: Cheering for both teams is trying to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds.
wrong_sentence: Run with the hare and hunt with the hounds means you pick one side and stay there.

meaning: very drunk
nomenclature_reason: Sailors call a loose sail a 'sheet'; when three of them are loose the ship spins wildly, just like a drunk person stumbling.
example: After the party, Jake was three sheets to the wind and could barely stand.
remember: Loose sails make a wobbling ship, like a drunk wobbling on land.
correct_sentence: After too much punch he was three sheets to the wind and could not walk straight.
wrong_sentence: Three sheets to the wind means you are wide awake and perfectly steady.

idiom: caught between the devil and the deep blue sea
meaning: stuck between two dangerous choices
nomenclature_reason: Imagine being trapped between a scary devil and a dangerous ocean-both are frightening, so you feel trapped.
example: She was caught between the devil and the deep blue sea, having to choose between moving away or staying with her sick mother.
remember: Two scary sides, no easy way out.
correct_sentence: Stay with a sick friend or make the recital: she was caught between the devil and the deep blue sea.
wrong_sentence: Caught between the devil and the deep blue sea means both choices are safe and easy.

meaning: very neat and orderly
nomenclature_reason: Sailors from Bristol were famous for keeping their ships tidy; 'shipshape' means tidy, so the whole phrase means perfectly neat.
example: The classroom was shipshape and Bristol fashion after everyone helped clean.
remember: A tidy room is shipshape and Bristol fashion.
correct_sentence: After the cleanup the art room was shipshape and Bristol fashion.
wrong_sentence: Shipshape and Bristol fashion means the room is messy and out of order.

meaning: a hard test that shows if you can handle something
nomenclature_reason: In old times people were tested by being put near fire; today it means a very tough challenge.
example: His first day at the new job was a trial by fire.
remember: A big challenge is a trial by fire.
correct_sentence: Leading the first assembly was a trial by fire.
wrong_sentence: A trial by fire is an easy warm-up that does not test you.

meaning: be forced to accept a punishment or danger
nomenclature_reason: Pirates made prisoners walk off a wooden board into the sea as a scary punishment.
example: When the team lost the game, the coach made them walk the plank and do extra drills.
remember: Being made to do something scary is like walking the plank.
correct_sentence: After the loss the coach made them walk the plank with extra laps.
wrong_sentence: Walk the plank means receive a reward for a job well done.

meaning: wishing someone good luck and smooth travel
nomenclature_reason: Sailors hope the wind blows from behind and the sea moves with them, giving an easy journey.
example: Before the school trip, the teacher said, 'Fair wind and following seas!'
remember: Good wishes for a smooth journey.
correct_sentence: As the bus left, the coach called, fair wind and following seas.
wrong_sentence: Fair wind and following seas is a warning that the trip will go badly.

meaning: following the exact wording, not the spirit
nomenclature_reason: A 'letter' is a written rule; taking it literally means no flexibility, just the words.
example: The librarian followed the letter of the law and wouldn't let anyone copy books.
remember: Reading every word, not the meaning.
correct_sentence: She followed the letter of the law and refused a late pass even for a good reason.
wrong_sentence: The letter of the law means you follow the purpose of a rule, not its exact words.

meaning: the intention behind a rule, not just the words
nomenclature_reason: The 'spirit' is the feeling or purpose behind the written rule, like the heart of the law.
example: The teacher applied the spirit of the law by letting the sick student take the test later.
remember: What the rule really wants.
correct_sentence: Letting the sick student test later followed the spirit of the law.
wrong_sentence: The spirit of the law means you obey only the exact words and ignore the purpose.

meaning: something that gives you energy or confidence
nomenclature_reason: A ship moves faster when the wind fills its sails, giving it a boost.
example: Winning the prize gave her wind in her sails for the next competition.
remember: A boost that pushes you forward.
correct_sentence: The kind note put wind in her sails before the next match.
wrong_sentence: Wind in her sails means something that leaves her tired and unsure.

meaning: a quiet period before trouble starts
nomenclature_reason: Before a storm, the air often feels still and quiet.
example: The playground was quiet-a calm before the storm of recess.
remember: Quiet now, trouble soon.
correct_sentence: The quiet hallway was the calm before the storm of recess.
wrong_sentence: The calm before the storm means the trouble is already over.

meaning: something very hard to find
nomenclature_reason: Looking for a tiny needle among lots of hay is almost impossible, just like a very hard search.
example: Finding my lost earring was like looking for a needle in a haystack.
remember: Tiny thing in a huge pile.
correct_sentence: Finding one blue bead in the gym was like finding a needle in a haystack.
wrong_sentence: A needle in a haystack is something sitting in plain sight.

idiom: separate the wheat from the chaff
meaning: distinguish valuable things from worthless ones
nomenclature_reason: Farmers shake grain to let the light chaff blow away, keeping only the good wheat.
example: The teacher helped us separate the wheat from the chaff in the story.
remember: Find the good stuff, leave the junk.
correct_sentence: Sorting real facts from rumors helped us separate the wheat from the chaff.
wrong_sentence: Separate the wheat from the chaff means mix the useful and the useless together.

meaning: a general guideline based on experience
nomenclature_reason: Old carpenters used their thumb to measure roughly, giving a quick, practical rule.
example: A good rule of thumb is to wash your hands before meals.
remember: A simple helpful rule.
correct_sentence: A good rule of thumb is to pack a pencil for every test.
wrong_sentence: A rule of thumb is a law written in a book that never bends.

meaning: a warning of bad weather or trouble ahead
nomenclature_reason: Sailors noticed that a red sunrise often meant a storm was coming, so it became a warning.
example: The dark clouds and red sky at morning told us to stay inside.
remember: Red sunrise means watch out.
correct_sentence: That red sky at morning told the sailors a storm was coming.
wrong_sentence: Red sky at morning means the day ahead will be calm and bright.

meaning: information that comes directly from the original source
nomenclature_reason: We picture hearing news straight from the horse that was told, so it's the most reliable way to hear it
example: I heard the news straight from the horse's mouth, so it's definitely true.
remember: If you want the real story, hear it straight from the horse's mouth.
correct_sentence: I heard the date straight from the horse's mouth, from the coach herself.
wrong_sentence: Straight from the horse's mouth means you heard a rumor from a stranger.

meaning: to do something pointless because that place already has plenty of it
nomenclature_reason: Newcastle once had so much coal that bringing more coal there was a wasted trip.
example: Giving the librarian another book about libraries was like carrying coals to Newcastle.
remember: Do not bring extra coal to a town that is already full of coal.
correct_sentence: Bringing sand to the beach is carrying coals to Newcastle.
wrong_sentence: Carry coals to Newcastle means bring something the place badly needs.

meaning: to become ruined or decline
nomenclature_reason: When something 'goes to the dogs,' it ends up in a messy, uncontrolled state
example: The old playground has gone to the dogs and needs repair.
remember: When things fall apart, they go to the dogs.
correct_sentence: The old garden has gone to the dogs and the paths are full of weeds.
wrong_sentence: Go to the dogs means a place becomes cleaner and more popular.

meaning: a threat of poverty or danger knocking
nomenclature_reason: A hungry wolf at your door means trouble is coming close
example: With the bills unpaid, the wolf at the door was loud.
remember: When trouble knocks, it's the wolf at the door.
correct_sentence: With rent due, they could hear the wolf at the door.
wrong_sentence: The wolf at the door means plenty of money and no worry ahead.

meaning: an obvious problem that people ignore
nomenclature_reason: An elephant is huge, so it's hard to miss, yet people pretend not to see it
example: Nobody talked about the broken window; it was the elephant in the room.
remember: A big issue we ignore is the elephant in the room.
correct_sentence: Nobody mentioned the cracked trophy; it was the elephant in the room.
wrong_sentence: The elephant in the room is a tiny problem nobody has noticed.

meaning: to do something impossible, often said when you're sure something won't happen
nomenclature_reason: It imagines someone actually eating a hat, which is absurd, so it shows how unlikely the event is
example: If I ever finish all my homework early, I'll eat my hat.
remember: Eating a hat means something is so unlikely you'll only do it if it really happens.
correct_sentence: If that quiet kid ever shouts in class, I will eat my hat.
wrong_sentence: Eat one's hat means you expect something to happen and it does.

meaning: to apologize and accept that you were wrong
nomenclature_reason: In old times, "humble pie" was a lowly dish, so eating it means accepting a low position
example: After bragging about the game, Maya had to eat humble pie when she lost.
remember: Eating humble pie is like saying sorry and learning your lesson.
correct_sentence: After boasting, he had to eat humble pie when he lost.
wrong_sentence: Eat humble pie means celebrate because you were right all along.

idiom: have a bun in the oven
meaning: to be pregnant
nomenclature_reason: A bun baking in an oven is like a baby growing inside a mother
example: Grandma whispered that Aunt Lily has a bun in the oven.
remember: A bun in the oven means a baby is on the way.
correct_sentence: Aunt Rosa has a bun in the oven and is expecting a baby in spring.
wrong_sentence: Have a bun in the oven means a loaf of bread is baking for dinner.

meaning: to be the person who makes the decisions, usually in a family
nomenclature_reason: Long ago, the person who wore trousers (often the man) was seen as the boss
example: Even though Mom works, she still wears the trousers at home.
remember: Wearing the trousers means being the boss.
correct_sentence: In that house, Dad wears the trousers and picks the weekend plans.
wrong_sentence: Wear the trousers means you own a pair of pants and nothing more.

meaning: to keep a secret
nomenclature_reason: Hiding something under a hat keeps it out of sight, just like a secret
example: The surprise party is a secret; keep it under your hat.
remember: Something under the hat stays hidden.
correct_sentence: The surprise is a secret, so keep it under your hat.
wrong_sentence: Keep it under your hat means tell the secret to everyone you meet.

meaning: to dress very elegantly and fashionably
nomenclature_reason: The phrase suggests being dressed as finely as the number nine, a perfect score
example: For the royal ball, the princess will dress to the nines.
remember: Dress to the nines means looking your very best.
correct_sentence: For the concert she will dress to the nines in her best coat.
wrong_sentence: Dress to the nines means wear your oldest, plainest clothes.

idiom: make a silk purse out of a sow's ear
meaning: to turn something poor into something valuable
nomenclature_reason: A sow's ear is rough, a silk purse is fine; turning one into the other shows great skill
example: The carpenter made a silk purse out of a sow's ear by turning old wood into a beautiful table.
remember: Making a silk purse out of a sow's ear means changing something plain into something precious.
correct_sentence: Turning scrap wood into a bookshelf is making a silk purse out of a sow's ear.
wrong_sentence: Make a silk purse out of a sow's ear means ruin something that was already fine.

meaning: to maintain a warm, comfortable household, especially during hard times
nomenclature_reason: In old houses, a fire in the hearth kept the home warm; keeping it burning means caring for the family
example: While Grandpa was away, Mom kept the home fires burning.
remember: Keeping the home fires burning means caring for your family.
correct_sentence: While he was away at camp, his sister kept the home fires burning.
wrong_sentence: Keep the home fires burning means let the house go cold and empty.

idiom: lock the stable door after the horse has bolted
meaning: to try to prevent something after it's already happened; too late
nomenclature_reason: If the horse has already run away, locking the stable door doesn't help
example: She tried to apologize after the vase broke, but it was like locking the stable door after the horse had bolted.
remember: Locking the stable door after the horse has bolted means it's too late.
correct_sentence: Apologizing after the vase shattered was locking the stable door after the horse has bolted.
wrong_sentence: Lock the stable door after the horse has bolted means you stopped the problem in time.

meaning: to hide a problem instead of dealing with it
nomenclature_reason: Sweeping dust under a rug hides it from view, just like ignoring an issue
example: The kids tried to sweep the broken toy under the rug instead of fixing it.
remember: Sweeping under the rug hides the mess.
correct_sentence: They tried to sweep the broken mug under the rug instead of telling anyone.
wrong_sentence: Sweep something under the rug means clean it up and deal with it openly.

idiom: have a roof over one's head
meaning: to have a place to live; shelter
nomenclature_reason: A roof protects you from rain and wind, showing you have a home
example: Even after the storm, we were grateful to have a roof over our heads.
remember: A roof over your head means you have a home.
correct_sentence: After the move we were glad to have a roof over our heads.
wrong_sentence: A roof over one's head means you have nowhere to sleep tonight.

idiom: be as snug as a bug in a rug
meaning: to be very comfortable and warm
nomenclature_reason: A bug tucked into a rug is cozy and safe
example: The kitten curled up and was as snug as a bug in a rug.
remember: As snug as a bug in a rug means very cozy.
correct_sentence: Wrapped in the quilt, the puppy was as snug as a bug in a rug.
wrong_sentence: As snug as a bug in a rug means cold, cramped, and uncomfortable.

idiom: be as clean as a whistle
meaning: to be perfectly clean or pure
nomenclature_reason: A whistle makes a clear sound; being as clean as a whistle suggests spotless
example: After washing the dishes, the kitchen was as clean as a whistle.
remember: As clean as a whistle means sparkling clean.
correct_sentence: The washed windows were as clean as a whistle.
wrong_sentence: As clean as a whistle means still smudged and dusty.

meaning: to suffer a final and decisive defeat, especially after a long period of success
nomenclature_reason: The Battle of Waterloo was where Napoleon was finally beaten, so meeting it means meeting defeat
example: After losing the final match, the champion finally met his Waterloo.
remember: Think of the famous battle that stopped a great leader.
correct_sentence: The long winning streak ended when she met her Waterloo in the final.
wrong_sentence: Meet one's Waterloo means win the biggest victory of your life.

meaning: to die while still active, often in battle or while doing something you love
nomenclature_reason: Soldiers wear boots in battle, so dying with them on means dying on the battlefield
example: The brave explorer died with his boots on, climbing the highest mountain.
remember: If you're still wearing your boots, you're still in the fight.
correct_sentence: The gardener wanted to die with his boots on, still planting trees.
wrong_sentence: Die with one's boots on means stop working and rest for years first.

meaning: to keep trying even though success is almost impossible
nomenclature_reason: A battle that cannot be won still looks like a fight, so the phrase warns against futile effort
example: She kept arguing with the bully, but it was a losing battle.
remember: Sometimes fighting is brave, even if you can't win.
correct_sentence: Arguing with the closed gate was fighting a losing battle.
wrong_sentence: Fight a losing battle means the win is almost certain if you keep going.

meaning: to fail spectacularly and dramatically
nomenclature_reason: When a plane crashes, it often bursts into flames, showing a dramatic failure
example: The new toy went down in flames after the first use.
remember: A big, bright failure looks like a fire in the sky.
correct_sentence: The cardboard rocket went down in flames on its first launch.
wrong_sentence: Go down in flames means succeed in a quiet, modest way.

meaning: to keep a firm position and not give up
nomenclature_reason: In battle soldiers stand on a line and must not let enemies break through
example: Even when the game got hard, she held the line and kept playing.
remember: Imagine soldiers staying strong on a straight line.
correct_sentence: Even when the score fell behind, she held the line.
wrong_sentence: Hold the line means give up your spot as soon as it gets hard.

meaning: a mercenary; someone who fights for pay rather than loyalty
nomenclature_reason: A soldier who works for fortune (money) fights for whoever pays him
example: The adventure story featured a soldier of fortune who traveled the world.
remember: Think of a brave fighter who follows the gold.
correct_sentence: The story's hero was a soldier of fortune who fought only for pay.
wrong_sentence: A soldier of fortune fights only for loyalty to a home country.

meaning: to fight very fiercely and with all your strength
nomenclature_reason: Using both teeth and nails suggests using every possible weapon, even the smallest
example: The team fought tooth and nail to win the championship.
remember: Picture a fierce animal using its teeth and claws.
correct_sentence: They fought tooth and nail to keep the club open.
wrong_sentence: Fight tooth and nail means argue gently and give up quickly.

meaning: a heated argument where people exchange angry statements
nomenclature_reason: Instead of swords, people use words as weapons in a conflict
example: The two friends had a war of words after the misunderstanding.
remember: Imagine a battle where the weapons are spoken words.
correct_sentence: The captains had a war of words over who should kick first.
wrong_sentence: A war of words is a calm chat where nobody raises a voice.

meaning: a contest where people try to outsmart each other
nomenclature_reason: Wits are clever thoughts; a battle of wits is a mental fight
example: The riddles turned the game into a battle of wits.
remember: Think of a chess match where brains are the swords.
correct_sentence: The riddle contest became a battle of wits.
wrong_sentence: A battle of wits is a contest decided by who can run fastest.

meaning: a long conflict that wears down the opponent slowly
nomenclature_reason: Attrition means wearing away; a war of attrition wears down both sides over time
example: The long school project became a war of attrition for the team.
remember: Imagine a battle that lasts so long it makes everyone tired.
correct_sentence: The month-long debate turned into a war of attrition.
wrong_sentence: A war of attrition ends in one quick moment.

meaning: a struggle where each side tries to outlast the other's patience or courage
nomenclature_reason: Nerves are bravery; a war of nerves tests who can stay calm the longest
example: During the game, the players entered a war of nerves, waiting for the other to slip.
remember: Picture two knights trying not to blink first.
correct_sentence: The penalty kicks became a war of nerves.
wrong_sentence: A war of nerves is a contest of who can lift the heaviest weight.

meaning: to be experienced, reliable, and often used many times, especially in performance or work
nomenclature_reason: Warhorses carried soldiers into many battles, showing strength and endurance
example: The actor became a warhorse, starring in play after play.
remember: Think of a sturdy horse that never gets tired.
correct_sentence: After twenty plays, the actor was a warhorse the school could count on.
wrong_sentence: A warhorse is a beginner who has never been on stage.

meaning: to act with honesty, fairness, and respect for promises
nomenclature_reason: Honor is a knight's badge; a man who carries it follows a noble code
example: He returned the lost wallet because he wanted to be a man of honor.
remember: Imagine a knight keeping his shining badge of honor.
correct_sentence: He returned the wallet because he wanted to be a man of honor.
wrong_sentence: A man of honor keeps a promise only when it is easy.

meaning: to do exactly what you promised
nomenclature_reason: A word is like a promise; keeping it shows trustworthiness
example: She promised to help and kept her word.
remember: Treat your promise like a treasure you never lose.
correct_sentence: She said she would bring the balls, and she kept her word.
wrong_sentence: Keep one's word means promise something and then forget it.

meaning: to refuse to move or give up, especially when faced with pressure
nomenclature_reason: In battle, soldiers stand firm on the ground to protect their position
example: Even when the wind blew hard, the little tree stood its ground.
remember: Picture a brave soldier who never steps back.
correct_sentence: When they teased her idea, she stood her ground.
wrong_sentence: Stand one's ground means step aside the moment someone disagrees.

meaning: Life is like a play where everyone has a role.
nomenclature_reason: Shakespeare compared life to a theater stage, so we picture people acting like actors.
example: When Sam moved to a new school, his teacher reminded him that all the world's a stage and he could make new friends.
remember: Think of life as a big stage where you get to act.
correct_sentence: Starting at a new school, he remembered that all the world's a stage.
wrong_sentence: All the world's a stage means life has no roles and nobody is watching.

meaning: Even if something bad happens, we keep continuing.
nomenclature_reason: In theater, the performance continues no matter what problems arise.
example: Even after the power went out, the kids sang loudly because the show must go on.
remember: Keep going, just like a performance that never stops.
correct_sentence: The microphone died, but the show must go on.
wrong_sentence: The show must go on means cancel everything when one thing goes wrong.

meaning: Do something just to impress people watching.
nomenclature_reason: In old theatres, the gallery was the cheap seats where actors tried to wow the crowd.
example: Lily told a funny story at dinner just to play to the gallery.
remember: Imagine acting for the audience in the cheap seats.
correct_sentence: He told the joke only to play to the gallery.
wrong_sentence: Play to the gallery means perform for yourself and ignore the crowd.

meaning: Attract all the attention away from others.
nomenclature_reason: Limelight was a bright stage light; stealing it means taking the brightest spot.
example: When the magician performed his trick, he stole the limelight from the other acts.
remember: Picture grabbing the brightest stage light for yourself.
correct_sentence: Her solo stole the limelight from the rest of the band.
wrong_sentence: Steal the limelight means stay in the back so others get the attention.

meaning: Accept praise after doing something well.
nomenclature_reason: Actors bow at the end of a performance to thank the audience.
example: After winning the spelling bee, Maya took a bow and thanked her teacher.
remember: Think of bowing after a great show.
correct_sentence: After the winning goal she took a bow.
wrong_sentence: Take a bow means refuse any praise and leave quietly.

meaning: Look carefully at the small details before agreeing.
nomenclature_reason: Printed contracts have tiny words that hold important rules.
example: Before joining the club, Jake read the fine print to see the meeting times.
remember: Look at the tiny words, just like a detective.
correct_sentence: Before he signed, he read the fine print about practice days.
wrong_sentence: Read the fine print means glance at the title and skip the details.

meaning: Agreeing or understanding each other.
nomenclature_reason: When people read the same page of a book, they share the same story.
example: The science project partners were on the same page about the experiment steps.
remember: Imagine reading the same page together.
correct_sentence: The partners were on the same page about the experiment.
wrong_sentence: On the same page means you disagree about every step.

meaning: Prepare something carefully before it is used.
nomenclature_reason: Old printers arranged metal letters (type) before printing a page.
example: Before the play, the director set the type for the script notes.
remember: Think of arranging letters before printing.
correct_sentence: Before the show, the director set the type for the cue cards.
wrong_sentence: Set the type means start using something before it is prepared.

meaning: Sign an agreement officially.
nomenclature_reason: People used ink to write contracts, making the deal real.
example: The two schools inked a deal to share library books.
remember: Picture signing with a big ink pen.
correct_sentence: The two clubs inked a deal to share the field.
wrong_sentence: Ink a deal means talk about an agreement and never sign it.

meaning: A person who is very learned and reads a lot.
nomenclature_reason: Letters are the building blocks of books, so a man of letters loves them.
example: Grandpa is a man of letters; his shelves are full of classic novels.
remember: Think of someone surrounded by many letters.
correct_sentence: Grandpa is a man of letters, always in the middle of a classic novel.
wrong_sentence: A man of letters is someone who rarely reads and avoids books.

meaning: Very quick and sharp at understanding or remembering.
nomenclature_reason: A steel trap snaps shut fast, just like a quick mind.
example: When the quiz started, Maya's mind was like a steel trap and she answered everything.
remember: Imagine a fast-snapping steel trap in your head.
correct_sentence: At the quiz her mind was like a steel trap.
wrong_sentence: A mind like a steel trap forgets names and dates right away.

meaning: Better than everyone else.
nomenclature_reason: If you cut a piece higher than the others, it stands out.
example: Lila's artwork was a cut above the rest in the school exhibition.
remember: Think of a piece that sticks out higher.
correct_sentence: Her model bridge was a cut above the rest.
wrong_sentence: A cut above the rest means about the same as everyone else.

meaning: A source that provides a lot of information.
nomenclature_reason: A fountain constantly flows water; a fountain of knowledge constantly flows facts.
example: The library is a fountain of knowledge for curious kids.
remember: Imagine a water fountain spilling out books.
correct_sentence: The librarian is a fountain of knowledge about local history.
wrong_sentence: A fountain of knowledge is a person with very little to share.

meaning: to trick someone with a story that is obviously false
nomenclature_reason: Long ago, tricksters pretended they could sell a famous bridge that was not theirs.
example: His email about free gold was just selling the Brooklyn Bridge.
remember: Nobody can really sell you a bridge the city already owns.
correct_sentence: The email about free gold was just selling the Brooklyn Bridge.
wrong_sentence: Sell the Brooklyn Bridge means offer a deal everyone can check and trust.

meaning: a situation where people cannot understand each other because of confusion
nomenclature_reason: In the Bible, people tried to build a tower to reach heaven, but God confused their languages, making the tower a symbol of chaos
example: The classroom became a tower of Babel when everyone tried to speak at once.
remember: A tower of Babel is a big mess of mixed-up words.
correct_sentence: When every group shouted a different plan, the room was a tower of Babel.
wrong_sentence: A tower of Babel is a meeting where everyone understands each other at once.

meaning: be careful of people who offer something that seems kind but may hide danger
nomenclature_reason: In the tale of Troy, the Greeks pretended to give a gift, a wooden horse, which actually held soldiers inside
example: The new game looked fun, but Mom said, "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts; sometimes freebies have hidden costs"
remember: If a gift feels too good, remember the Greeks' trick
correct_sentence: The free game looked fun, but beware of Greeks bearing gifts.
wrong_sentence: Beware of Greeks bearing gifts means every kind offer is safe to accept.

meaning: to be hurt by the very plan you made yourself
nomenclature_reason: A petard was a tiny bomb used to break down walls; if it exploded and lifted the person who set it, they were 'hoisted' by their own bomb.
example: Tom tried to set a prank on his brother, but the prank backfired and Tom was hoist with his own petard.
remember: If your trick blows up on you, you're hoist with your own petard.
correct_sentence: His own prank tripped him, so he was hoist with his own petard.
wrong_sentence: Hoist with one's own petard means your clever plan works exactly as you hoped.

meaning: A rule that is clearly established and widely accepted in law.
nomenclature_reason: In old legal books, the most important rules were printed in bold black letters so everyone could see them easily.
example: The rule that you must stop at a red light is black letter law.
remember: Think of a rule written in bold black letters-it's a black letter law!
correct_sentence: Stopping for a red light is black letter law.
wrong_sentence: Black letter law means a rule nobody is sure about.

meaning: something that looks exciting for a moment and then disappears
nomenclature_reason: Old guns sometimes flashed in the pan without firing the shot.
example: The magic trick was a flash in the pan, and everyone forgot it the next day.
remember: A quick flash is not the same as a real shot.
correct_sentence: The sudden dance craze was a flash in the pan and faded by Friday.
wrong_sentence: A flash in the pan is a success that lasts for years.
